chapters.title: Search Engine Optimization (SEO) Starter Guide
chapters.takeaway: Help Google discover and understand useful content, and help people decide whether it answers their needs. Technical eligibility and sensible optimization improve opportunities; they never guarantee indexing or first place.
notes: Purpose, eligibility, and expectations
SEO helps search engines understand content and helps people find a site and decide whether to visit. Google treats a search engine as one of the website's users.

Search Essentials establishes eligibility. Following it makes inclusion more likely, but no particular website is guaranteed a place in the index. There is no secret that automatically produces a number-one ranking.
Google is automated: publishing accessible content is usually enough for eventual discovery. Most listed websites are found through crawling rather than manual submission.

The guide's recommendations depend on the business. Some changes can be reflected in hours; others take months. Google generally recommends allowing a few weeks before assessing whether an optimization helped. A change may produce no noticeable effect; iterate when business constraints permit.
Discovery and seeing what Google sees

First check whether Google already knows the site. A site: search showing your pages confirms that those returned pages are in the index. If no results appear, investigate technical requirements. This is an initial check, not a complete URL-level diagnostic; use URL Inspection for a specific URL.
Google primarily discovers new pages from links on already known pages, including external websites. Promotion can help people discover content and subsequently link to it.

A sitemap lists URLs you care about and can be submitted; a CMS may generate one. It is useful but is not a universal requirement or an indexing guarantee. Do not ignore discoverable links or audience awareness.
Let Google access important CSS, JavaScript, and other resources so its rendered view resembles an ordinary visitor's. Blocking these can damage understanding and visibility.
Location-dependent pages need special attention: Googlebot generally crawls from the US. Check that the content served from its location is the version you intend Google to see.

Use Search Console's URL Inspection to inspect Google's view. The guide also points to separate methods for keeping files, directories, or a whole website out of crawling or indexing; choose the mechanism for the actual objective.
Logical architecture and descriptive URLs

Logical organization helps users and search engines understand relationships between pages. Google does not tell every established website to restructure immediately; prioritize changes that justify their cost.
Use descriptive words in URLs for users. URL words can inform breadcrumbs, and breadcrumb structured data can influence their presentation. /pets/cats.html communicates more than a random identifier.

On sites with more than a few thousand URLs, grouping related pages into directories can help Google learn different update patterns. Policy pages may change rarely while promotions change frequently; Google can crawl these groups at different frequencies.

Duplicate content means substantially the same information under different URLs. Google selects a canonical representative. Routine duplication on your own website is not itself a spam-policy violation, but it can confuse users and consume crawling resources.

Prefer one URL per piece of content when feasible. Redirect redundant URLs to the preferred version when users should go there; use a rel="canonical" link element when redirects are unsuitable. Google can also canonicalize without an explicit declaration. Copying other publishers' content is a different issue.
Useful content, search language, ads, and links

Useful, compelling content is likely to matter more than the other improvements in this guide. Write naturally, organize paragraphs and sections, use helpful headings, and correct spelling and grammar.
Contribute original content rather than copying or rehashing. Review older pages, update when necessary, and remove material that no longer serves a relevant purpose.
Make information helpful, reliable, and intended for readers. Expert or experienced sources can demonstrate the knowledge behind the article.

Understand how novices and specialists describe the same need, such as cheese board versus charcuterie. You need not include every keyword variant; Google's language systems can understand relevance without the exact query wording.
Advertising should not distract so heavily that it prevents use of the content. Interstitials that obstruct expected content are an example to watch.
Internal and external links support discovery and supply context or corroboration. Anchor text should explain the target page so users and search engines can anticipate what they will find.

Link to sources you trust. For a link you cannot endorse, use nofollow or a similar qualification. User-posted links should receive suitable qualifications automatically to discourage spam and avoid blindly associating your site with their destinations.
Titles, snippets, images, and video

The title link is the search result's headline. Google may generate it from the HTML title element and other headings; your title is an input, not a promise of exact display. CMS software often creates the title element automatically.
Good titles are unique, concise, descriptive, and accurate. Include a business name, location, or relevant offering when useful. This page gives no mandatory character limit.

A snippet is the descriptive text beneath a title link. It is generally drawn from page content and can sometimes come from the meta description. Write a short, page-specific description summarizing the important information; do not assume it will always be displayed.

Images can be an independent discovery channel. Use sharp, clear images near text that explains their relevant context. A yarn-store image belongs near the corresponding store's location and review information.
Alt text briefly describes how the image relates to the page. Add it with an img element's alt attribute or the CMS field; write a meaningful description rather than a keyword list.

For video-led pages, create a high-quality video and a standalone watch page with relevant supporting text. Use descriptive video titles and descriptions. Video-heavy websites should follow the linked specialist guidance too.
Promotion and the complete myth list

Promote content through social channels, communities, online and offline advertising, and word of mouth. Include the URL in business cards, stationery, posters, and other business materials. Newsletters are suggested with the recipients' permission.
Promotion can improve discovery; overpromotion can fatigue people, and manipulative practices can be seen as search spam.
Meta keywords: Google Search does not use the keywords meta tag.
Keyword stuffing: excessive repetition, including variations, violates Google's spam policies.
Keywords in domains or URL paths: alone they have hardly any ranking effect beyond their appearance in breadcrumbs. Choose names for the business and users.
TLDs: generally not important to Google; country targeting can make a country-code TLD relevant, usually as a low-impact signal. A generic .com does not automatically outrank .org or .asia.
Content length: there is no magical minimum, maximum, or target word count for ranking. Natural breadth may cover more relevant language; padding has no inherent value.
Subdomains versus subdirectories: choose what makes organizational and business sense. The guide does not declare a universal ranking winner.
PageRank: links matter and PageRank is one fundamental algorithm, but it is only one among many ranking signals.
Duplicate-content penalty: ordinary duplication under multiple URLs does not itself cause a manual action. Distinguish inefficiency from copying other sites or spam.
Headings: semantic order is valuable for screen readers; Google does not require an ideal heading count or perfect order. Avoid unnecessary excess for users.
E-E-A-T: it is not a single ranking factor. See the helpful-content chapter for the full distinction.
Next steps and staying current
Set up Search Console and learn the relevant reports. Maintain SEO over time, including migrations and multilingual configurations.
Appropriate valid structured data can make pages eligible for special search appearances. Eligibility does not guarantee display.
Keep up with Google Search Central's blog, LinkedIn, X, YouTube, and Help Forum. The forum includes Product Experts and sometimes Googlers.

chapters.title: In-depth guide to how Google Search works
chapters.takeaway: Separate URL discovery, crawling, indexing, and serving. An accessible URL can be discovered without being crawled, crawled without being indexed, or indexed without appearing for a particular query.
notes: Automation and the three stages
Google finds most pages automatically using crawlers. Manual submission is not the usual route into Search.

The three named stages are crawling, indexing, and serving search results. URL discovery is explained within the crawling stage; rendering is part of processing fetched content, not a fourth named stage in this article.
Google accepts no payment for more frequent crawling or higher organic rankings. Compliance with Search Essentials does not guarantee crawling, indexing, or serving.
Crawling: discovery, scheduling, access, and rendering

There is no central registry of every web page. Google continually discovers new and updated URLs from previous visits, links extracted from known pages, and submitted sitemaps. A category hub linking to a new article is one example.
Discovering a URL does not mean Google will fetch it. Googlebot chooses which sites to crawl, how often, and how many pages using an algorithmic process.
Crawlers avoid overloading servers. Server responses affect behavior; HTTP 500 errors can cause crawling to slow down. Infrastructure health matters independently of content quality.
Some discovered URLs are blocked from crawling or require authentication. Common crawl access problems are server issues, network issues, and robots.txt rules.

Google renders pages and runs JavaScript using a recent Chrome version. Rendering helps expose content produced by scripts. A page that appears complete to a logged-in human can still present incomplete content to Google.
Indexing: understanding, clustering, and canonical selection
Google analyzes page text, title elements, image alt attributes, images, videos, and other information to understand a crawled page.

Similar pages are grouped into clusters, and Google selects a canonical page that best represents each group. Other cluster members are alternate versions and may be served in particular contexts, such as a mobile user or a very specific request.

Google gathers signals about the canonical and its content, including language, geographic relevance, and usability. The resulting information may be stored in the index, a distributed database on thousands of computers.
Crawling and processing do not guarantee indexing. Reasons indexing can fail include low content quality, robots meta rules disallowing indexing, and a site design that makes understanding difficult.
Serving: relevance, context, and result types
When a query arrives, Google searches its index and returns what it considers relevant, high-quality results. Ranking is programmatic and involves hundreds of factors.
User location, language, and device can change relevance. A bicycle repair search can return different local businesses in Paris and Hong Kong.
Query needs also affect result features. A repair-shop search can show local results; a query for a modern bicycle may favor images. The article links to the visual-element gallery.

Search Console can show a page as indexed even when you cannot find it for a particular query. Possible reasons include weak query relevance, low quality, and serving restrictions from robots meta rules.
Google continuously improves its algorithms; the Search Central blog is the recommended update source.
Practical interpretation for an experienced candidate
Diagnose the failed stage before prescribing a fix. A blocked resource, missing discoverable link, non-indexable page, unintended canonical, and weak match to search intent are different problems.
Treat a recrawl request or sitemap as a discovery/processing aid, not a command to index or rank. Evidence from URL Inspection, the rendered page, and server logs makes the diagnosis more credible.
Those diagnosis steps are interview applications of the article; the article itself does not prescribe one universal troubleshooting checklist.

chapters.title: Creating helpful, reliable, people-first content
chapters.takeaway: Judge whether the page fulfills a real purpose for a real audience. Trust, original effort, useful evidence, and satisfaction matter; E-E-A-T and rater feedback are not direct numerical ranking scores.
notes: Self-assessment and auditing a decline
Google's automated systems seek helpful, reliable information created to benefit people rather than manipulate rankings.
Evaluate your own pages and obtain an honest assessment from trusted people who are not affiliated with the website. Avoid relying only on the team that produced the content.

If performance dropped, identify the affected pages and search types, then evaluate those pages against the actual questions. The guide recommends targeted assessment rather than declaring all content bad.
All twelve content-quality checks, paraphrased
Original contribution: does the page offer its own information, reporting, research, or analysis?
Completeness: does it explain the subject substantially and comprehensively enough for its purpose?
Insight: does it go beyond obvious information and offer useful analysis or discoveries?
Added value from sources: when drawing on other work, does it add originality and substantial value instead of merely copying or rewriting?
Descriptive title: does the main heading or title accurately and helpfully summarize the page?
Responsible title: does it avoid sensationalism, exaggeration, or shock as a substitute for value?
Recommendation value: would a reader bookmark it, share it, or recommend it?
Editorial credibility: is its quality comparable to material someone would expect in a book, encyclopedia, or print magazine?
Competitive value: does it offer substantial value compared with other search results?
Language care: are spelling and stylistic problems addressed?
Production care: does it look thoughtfully produced rather than rushed or sloppy?
Attention per page: has mass production, outsourcing, or publication across a large site network reduced the care given to individual pages?
All four expertise checks, paraphrased
Trust evidence: clear sourcing, proof of relevant knowledge, and background on the author or publisher, including appropriate author or About pages.
Reputation: would someone investigating the publisher see it as trusted or recognized in its subject?
Knowledgeable production or review: was the content written or reviewed by an expert or informed enthusiast?
Factual reliability: does it avoid errors that are easy to verify?
Page experience and all five people-first checks
Evaluate the overall experience rather than optimizing only one or two aspects. The guide refers readers to Google's separate page-experience documentation.
Audience: an existing or intended audience would find the page useful even if they arrived directly.
First-hand knowledge: the content demonstrates real experience, such as using a product, using a service, or visiting a place.
Focus: the website has a primary purpose or subject focus.
Goal completion: a reader learns enough to accomplish the intended task.
Satisfaction: the reader leaves feeling the experience was worthwhile.
All eleven search-engine-first warning signs
The main purpose is attracting search visits rather than helping an audience.
Publishing across many unrelated topics in the hope some pages rank.
Extensive automation across many topics.
Mainly summarizing other people's work without meaningful added value.
Choosing topics solely because they trend rather than because the audience needs them.
Readers must search again because the page did not adequately answer their need.
Writing to a supposedly preferred Google word count. Google says no such preference exists.
Entering a niche without real expertise because it appears to offer search traffic.
Promising an answer that is not known, such as an unconfirmed release date.
Changing displayed dates without substantial content changes to simulate freshness.
Adding many pages or removing old pages mainly to make the whole site appear fresh. The guide says this is not a general ranking improvement mechanism.
These are warning signs for reassessment, not a formula that proves a particular page has a penalty. SEO itself is useful when applied to people-first material to support discovery and understanding.
E-E-A-T, YMYL, and quality raters
E-E-A-T stands for experience, expertise, authoritativeness, and trustworthiness. Trust is the most important aspect; the other aspects support it.
Useful content need not demonstrate every aspect equally. First-hand experience can make one page valuable; specialist expertise can make another valuable.
E-E-A-T is not itself a specific ranking factor. Google's systems use a mixture of factors that can identify content exhibiting these qualities; do not invent an E-E-A-T score or fixed weight.
Strong E-E-A-T matters particularly for Your Money or Your Life topics that can significantly affect health, financial stability, safety, or societal welfare.

Quality raters assess whether Google's systems deliver good results, following the evaluator guidelines. They do not control page rankings, and their ratings are not directly used in ranking algorithms. Their feedback helps evaluate improvements to systems.
The guidelines can inform self-assessment; they are not an instruction manual for getting first place. They also emphasize how effectively main content fulfills a page's purpose.
Main content: definitions and all four quality attributes
Main content is any part of the page that directly achieves its purpose. It can include text, articles, images, audio, and videos.
It can also include working tools, calculators, games, and search features. A useful page is not necessarily an article.
User contributions can be main content when they fulfill the page's purpose, including forum discussions, customer reviews, comments, or uploaded media.

Tabbed and expandable information, such as product specifications, safety details, and reviews, can be main content. Visible titles and headings also qualify because they explain the page's subject and help users decide.

Effort: human work in the content or underlying system. Original analysis, a manual poem translation, and a custom game map illustrate effort. Automatically generated feed pages or large volumes of AI text without oversight illustrate little effort. Attribution alone does not replace original work.
Originality: unique information or perspectives beyond what other websites already provide.

Talent or skill: the ability required to deliver a satisfying result, such as clear writing, well-made videos, or functioning tools. Not every useful experience requires professional credentials; everyday practical experience can be valuable.
Accuracy: informational pages should be factually sound. YMYL content needs especially high accuracy and alignment with established expert consensus.
Who, How, and Why

Who: make actual authorship clear when expected. Add accurate bylines and relevant author-background links. Ask whether visitors can identify the author, whether a byline is present where appropriate, and whether it explains the creator's background.

Avoid fabricated expert identities, made-up names, false credentials, and AI headshots used to make nonexistent experts appear real. The guide explicitly identifies deceptive authorship as untrustworthy and a low-quality signal.
How: explain the production process when it matters. For reviews, show how many products were tested, how testing worked, what results were obtained, and evidence such as photos.

For substantial automation, assess whether it is apparent or disclosed, whether the process is explained, and why AI or automation was useful. Disclosures are useful when readers would reasonably ask how the material was created; this is not stated as a mandatory universal label for every page.

Why: the primary reason should be helping people, including people who arrive directly. The guide calls this the most important question. Automation used primarily to manipulate rankings violates the spam policies.

chapters.title: Optimizing your website for generative AI features on Google Search
chapters.takeaway: For Google AI Overviews and AI Mode, foundational SEO still applies. Build accessible, useful, distinctive content and verify eligibility. Avoid special-file, schema, keyword, or mention schemes sold as mandatory AI shortcuts.
notes: Relevance of SEO, RAG, and query fan-out
Google's generative AI features are rooted in its core Search ranking and quality systems. The guide treats optimization for these experiences as SEO.

Retrieval-augmented generation, also called grounding, retrieves relevant current pages from the Search index using core ranking systems. The response can use information from those pages and show clickable supporting links. This is different from assuming a model answers only from training memory.

Query fan-out generates related queries concurrently to find more information for the original request. For a weed-filled lawn, examples include herbicide selection, non-chemical removal, and preventing future weeds.

AEO means answer engine optimization; GEO means generative engine optimization. These are industry labels, not separate mandatory Google ranking frameworks. Evaluate providers against official guidance.
Distinctive content and reader satisfaction
The guide prioritizes unique, compelling, useful material. First-hand reviews and informed perspectives provide information a generic summary cannot.

Non-commodity content adds distinctive experience or expert insight beyond common knowledge. The guide contrasts a generic homebuyer tips list with a detailed account of a specific decision about an inspection and sewer line. The lesson is original evidence and insight, not a special headline formula.

Write well and organize content into paragraphs and sections with helpful headings. Relevant high-quality images and videos provide additional opportunities for discovery in AI experiences as well as ordinary Search.

Do not create separate pages for every possible query variant or fan-out request mainly to manipulate rankings or AI responses. That can violate scaled content abuse policy; page quantity is not a substitute for quality.

Google's systems can understand relevance without an exact query match. AI-assisted production still needs to meet Search Essentials and the spam policies. The decision test is whether a visitor would find the page helpful and satisfying.
Technical eligibility and access
A page must be indexed and eligible to appear in Google Search with a snippet. Meeting technical requirements and policies does not guarantee crawling, indexing, or selection for display.

The current article also says the site must be included in Search generative AI features through Search Console. Check the actual setting and inheritance rather than claiming that all indexed pages necessarily participate.
Maintain crawlable content and resources. Large, frequently changing sites may need crawl-budget work. Keep JavaScript implementations compatible with Google's access and rendering behavior.
Semantic HTML is useful, especially for screen-reader navigation; perfect semantic markup is not a requirement for AI visibility. Make content understandable and readable.

Provide a good experience across devices, reduce latency, and make the main content easy to distinguish. Reduce duplicate content where it wastes resources or confuses users. Verify the property in Search Console to support diagnosis.
Local and ecommerce details
Keep relevant Merchant Center product information, including feeds, and Google Business Profile information maintained. Generative AI responses can include local-business and product details.

The article also suggests considering Business Agent where it fits the business and its goals, describing a conversational Search experience that lets customers talk with the brand. This is an optional experience, not a universal SEO requirement.
All five AI-search myths

llms.txt and special files: Google Search does not use these files to improve visibility or rankings. They are not required. Creating them for another system that actually uses them is fine; this neither helps nor harms Google Search ranking. Google can crawl many file types without granting them special status.
Content chunking: no requirement to split content into tiny pieces. Google can understand multiple topics and identify relevant parts. Choose length and organization for the audience.
AI-specific rewriting: no required prose style or exhaustive long-tail keyword coverage. Synonyms and intent can be understood without exact wording.
Inauthentic mentions: manufacturing mentions across blogs, forums, or videos is not a supported path. AI features depend on core quality and spam systems too.
Special structured data: no mandatory AI schema.org markup. Normal applicable structured data remains useful for rich-result eligibility, but is not required for generative AI visibility.
Measurement, agents, and next steps

The current article directs readers to Search Console's Generative AI performance report for visibility. It also warns that third-party tools have no access to Google's internal ranking or AI systems.
AI agents can perform tasks on behalf of people, such as making reservations or comparing specifications. Browser agents may use screenshots, the DOM, and accessibility trees to understand a site.

The guide links to agent-friendly website practices and mentions the emerging Universal Commerce Protocol. Explore these if relevant and if time permits; do not confuse an emerging commerce protocol with a mandatory ranking factor.
Priorities are foundational technical SEO, unique audience-focused content, avoiding unsupported shortcuts, measuring visibility, and keeping informed about relevant agent experiences.

Follow the Search Central blog, social channels, Help Forum, and YouTube. The guide also notes that some content succeeds without overt SEO and that every listed recommendation is not a prerequisite for success.
Verified current detail from linked Search Console documentation

The Search generative AI control is under Settings > Search generative AI. Inclusion is the default for properties without an inherited choice; child properties can inherit or override a parent. Excluding affects the covered AI appearances, not ranking in other Search surfaces. This visibility control is distinct from AI-training controls. [S1]

The Search Generative AI performance report covers AI Overviews and AI Mode impressions, with pages, countries, dates, and devices; Discover has a separate report. Do not claim this report supplies AI clicks, CTR, or query-level data merely because ordinary Search performance does. The linked help pages say worldwide rollout occurred August 31, 2026. [S2]

chapters.title: Google Search's guidance on using generative AI content on your website
chapters.takeaway: AI can assist research and organization, but publishers remain responsible for accuracy, added value, and policy compliance. Review both visible content and generated metadata before publishing.
notes: Useful assistance versus scaled abuse
Generative AI can help research a subject and structure original work. Google does not describe AI assistance as automatically prohibited.
Generating many pages without value for users can violate scaled content abuse policy. All AI-assisted content must meet Search Essentials and the spam policies.

The article points to evaluator-guideline sections 4.6.5 for scaled content abuse and 4.6.6 for main content with little or no effort, originality, or added value. These are evaluation criteria, not a first-place ranking recipe; rater judgments do not directly determine rankings.
Accuracy, quality, relevance, and metadata

Generative models predict likely word sequences from training data; their output can contain inaccurate claims or hallucinations. The current guide explicitly calls manual fact-checking and review of all AI-generated content critical before publication.
Check truthfulness and trustworthiness, as well as relevance and overall quality. A grammatically polished output is not necessarily correct or useful.
Review generated title elements, meta descriptions, structured data, and image alt text too. These can influence or appear in Search; metadata can misrepresent content even when the body is accurate.
Structured data must satisfy the general guidelines and each applicable search feature's policies. Validate the markup to establish eligibility; validation does not guarantee rich-result display.
Context and ecommerce-specific requirements

Explain how content was produced when that helps the audience. Describe the role of automation and include relevant image metadata. The general Search guidance encourages appropriate context rather than declaring one required disclosure format for every page.

Merchant Center imposes specific rules: AI-generated images require IPTC DigitalSourceType metadata identifying TrainedAlgorithmicMedia. AI-generated product titles and descriptions must be supplied separately and identified as AI-generated.

Verified detail from the linked Merchant Center help page: use structured_title and structured_description with content and digital_source_type=trained_algorithmic_media for AI-generated text. Preserve applicable embedded source metadata on images. These are feed requirements, not a new schema.org type for ordinary article pages. [S3]
The article links to Google's AI-content blog FAQ for further explanation.
Practical publishing workflow (interview application)
Start from the audience's real question and an original contribution. Use AI for assistance, verify claims against reliable evidence, and obtain appropriate subject review.
Inspect every affected field, including metadata and product data. Validate structured markup, review the actual page, and disclose processes where readers reasonably need context.
Keep human oversight and added value proportional to the stakes. Do not sell this workflow as a fixed algorithmic ranking formula.

headings.text: Focus on accuracy, quality, and relevance

chapters.title: Maintaining your website's SEO
chapters.takeaway: Maintain SEO as the site changes: manage crawl and indexing controls, resources, duplicates, localization, migrations, search appearance, and the overall user experience. The current on-page title is Maintaining your website's SEO.
notes: Crawl and index controls, resources, and duplicates
Understand the crawl/index/serving pipeline before diagnosing problems. Learn how canonicals affect crawling and indexing.

Pages and essential resources must be accessible to an anonymous visitor and not blocked where Google needs them. The guide directs readers to URL Inspection for blocked resources and rendering checks; not every inaccessible item is visible in aggregate reporting.
robots.txt prevents crawling; it is not a reliable method of keeping a web page out of the index. Use noindex for index exclusion with crawling allowed, or require login for private material.

The article recommends avoiding unnecessary crawling of duplicates or unimportant resources when they create load. Do not block CSS or scripts needed to understand an important page. Separate resource access, canonical consolidation, and privacy objectives.
Sitemaps and international sites
Sitemaps communicate important URLs and support discovery, especially for changing content, media, and pages not easily discovered through links. Google may crawl URLs outside the sitemap.

Specific linked-guide clarification: Google ignores sitemap priority and changefreq values. It can use a lastmod value when consistently accurate and representative of a significant update. The general article's mention of update frequency is not proof that changefreq controls scheduling. [S4]

For multilingual or multiregional content, consult the specific guidance and use hreflang to communicate alternate language/locality versions. Locale-adaptive pages can be affected by the location from which Googlebot accesses them.
URL and whole-site migrations
For a permanent single-page move, implement a 301 redirect. For a temporary move, the article gives 302. Match the response to the actual intent rather than treating all redirects identically.
A removed page can use a helpful custom error page, but return a real HTTP 404. An error-like page returning a success response can be a soft 404.

For a whole-site move, implement required 301 redirects and sitemap changes and tell Google about the move using the appropriate migration process. The guide links to the full procedure; it does not promise instant transfer or unchanged traffic.
Every additional crawl/index practice named on the page

Make links crawlable. The broad article suggests nofollow for paid, login-restricted, or untrusted links. More specific current guidance prefers sponsored for paid placements and ugc for user contributions; nofollow remains acceptable for paid links and when other values do not apply. [S5]
Very large or rapidly changing sites can need crawl-budget management. Use important and updated sitemap URLs and appropriate blocks for content you do not want crawled.

The linked current crawl-budget guide describes capacity and demand and says its scale examples are rough, not hard thresholds. It includes roughly one million pages changing weekly, 10,000+ changing daily, or many discovered-but-unindexed URLs. Small sites already crawled promptly usually need routine sitemap and indexing checks. [S6]
Follow JavaScript SEO recommendations. For multipage articles, provide prominent crawlable next/previous links.
For infinite scrolling, supply a crawlable paginated alternative. Do not assume the crawler scrolls and clicks exactly like a visitor.
Block state-changing action URLs, such as posting comments, registering accounts, or adding to carts, from crawling with appropriate robots.txt rules.
Review Google's indexable file types. If crawling genuinely overloads the site, consult current crawl-rate guidance; this should be uncommon.
Migrate HTTP sites to HTTPS for user and publisher security.
Helping Google understand content
Put essential information in text rather than relying solely on graphics. Google can process many file types, but text is the safest way to communicate key information.
Appropriate structured data can clarify meaning and make pages eligible for rich results. Use relevant types and follow the developer guidelines.

The page mentions hand-authored markup, Structured Data Markup Helper, and Data Highlighter. It warns that highlighting can break after layout changes. These are options mentioned in the source, not a guarantee that every legacy interface will be available in every account.
Search Essentials and every content-specific category
Follow Search Essentials: some items are recommendations, while violations of applicable requirements or policies can lead to index removal. Do not describe every best practice as mandatory.
Video: follow video-specific crawling, discovery, and appearance guidance.

Images: follow image guidance and provide applicable metadata on the host page. The article specifically mentions a robots.txt Disallow rule to stop image indexing; distinguish this image-specific advice from web-page noindex behavior.
Children's content: the page directs readers to child-directed tagging and its linked COPPA guidance. This is the source's SEO/documentation pointer, not a complete legal-compliance checklist.
Adult content: appropriate tagging can support SafeSearch filtering.

News: consult Publisher Center documentation, provide a News sitemap, prevent abuse, review flexible sampling, mark subscription/paywalled content while enabling intended crawling, and use snippet/image controls as needed.
The page also mentions AMP and Web Stories as formats to consider. It does not make either a requirement for ranking or for all news publishers.
Experience, mobile, appearance, and Search Console

The page describes good experience as a priority and refers to it as a ranking consideration. Its helpful-content companion stresses evaluating the whole experience rather than only one or two metrics.

Use HTTPS; HTTP can be marked not secure in Chrome. Review performance using the Core Web Vitals report for site-level information and PageSpeed Insights for individual-page diagnostics. The article also mentions web.dev and AMP.
Mobile usability matters; Google uses a mobile crawler as the default for websites. Do not treat a strong desktop view as sufficient proof of what Google sees.

Explore suitable supported search features, provide a favicon and article date where applicable, improve title links and snippets, and use available controls when limiting snippet length or image/text previews is desired.
Use Search Console's reports to monitor and improve Search performance. The article links to the reporting guidance rather than prescribing one metric for every business.

chapters.title: Get started with Search: a developer's guide
chapters.takeaway: Search-friendly development means discoverable URLs, usable crawlable links, accessible text in the DOM, correct rendering, clear indexing controls, and accurate metadata. Inspect Google's view instead of assuming it matches the browser.
notes: Inspect Google, not just the human browser
Developer work should support relevant discovery while keeping the website secure, fast, accessible, and usable on all devices.
Use URL Inspection or Rich Results Test to understand Google's view. The article illustrates a browser displaying images that Google misses because of an unsupported JavaScript feature.
Googlebot discovers new and updated pages, but what a human sees does not prove the crawler has the same content or resources.
Links, sitemaps, and app URLs
Googlebot navigates by fetching and parsing links, sitemaps, and redirects. The page emphasizes that it should not depend on prior browsing context to understand the requested URL.
Use crawlable a elements and ensure every important page is reachable from another findable page. Link text, or alt text for an image link, should describe the destination.
Submit a sitemap describing important pages, media, files, and their relationships.
A single-page JavaScript application still needs a URL for each screen or piece of individual content. A browser-only state without a discoverable URL is insufficient as a search destination.
JavaScript, updates, and error evidence
Google executes JavaScript, but crawlers have differences and limitations in access and rendering. Follow the JavaScript SEO and troubleshooting guidance.
For new or changed content, submit sitemaps and use available recrawl requests. If indexing remains problematic, inspect server logs for errors.
These are ways to help Google discover and reprocess content, not a guarantee of indexing or immediate ranking.
Words, titles, descriptions, semantic HTML, and the DOM
Express important visual information in text. The article's product-category example shows why a grid of shirt images needs explanatory text rather than pictures alone.
Give each page a descriptive title and meta description that explain relevance. Unique accurate metadata supports useful search presentation.

Prefer semantic HTML for substantive content. The article notes that Google can index HTML, PDFs, images, and videos, while plugin-dependent material and canvas-rendered content are not indexed as ordinary page text.

Make meaningful text accessible in the DOM. Content inserted only through the CSS content property is not part of the DOM and is ignored by Google Search in the article's current wording. Decorative CSS text is fine; critical facts should be actual page content.

Do not turn the warning into the broader false claim that Google never processes video or image information; the other guides explicitly explain that media is analyzed. The practical requirement here is a reliable textual representation of important meaning.
Alternate versions and visibility controls
Google does not automatically know every mobile/desktop or international relationship. Consolidate duplicate URLs, identify localized versions, and make any applicable AMP alternatives discoverable.
Login or password protection restricts access. robots.txt blocks crawling. A noindex directive, with crawling allowed, prevents indexing.
Multiple controls can conflict. If Google cannot crawl a page, it may not see the noindex directive in that page. Choose coherent controls for the objective.
If intended content is missing from Search, use URL Inspection to check access, review robots.txt for unintentional blocks, and inspect HTML for noindex directives.
Rich results

Structured data provides explicit clues to page meaning and can support rich search appearances with styling, images, or interactive features. Explore the supported-feature gallery and choose an appropriate type.
Eligibility requires suitable content and compliant implementation; neither adding markup nor passing a test guarantees display.

Keep Google updated when content changes
Don't forget about the words on the page
Tell Google about other versions of your content
Enable rich results for your site

chapters.title: Do you need an SEO?
chapters.takeaway: A credible SEO understands the business, explains recommendations, follows Google's policies, gives realistic expectations, and measures useful outcomes. Google provides questions employers may directly reuse in your interview.
notes: Services, benefits, and risk
Hiring an SEO can improve visibility and save time, but irresponsible work can harm a website and its reputation. Assess both potential benefits and damage.

The listed services are content or structure review; technical advice on hosting, redirects, error pages, and JavaScript; content development; online business-development campaigns; keyword research; SEO training; market/geographic expertise; and optimization for generative AI.

Google advertising does not affect organic presence. Organic inclusion costs nothing, and Google does not accept payment for inclusion or ranking. Search Console, the official blog, and the forum are available information sources.
A small local business can often handle much of the work itself. Knowing the Starter Guide also helps a client evaluate a hired professional's recommendations.
Timing and all eight questions Google tells clients to ask
Engage an SEO early in a redesign or new-site launch to design search-friendly foundations. An existing site can also benefit.
Ask for examples of earlier work and success stories.
Ask whether the candidate follows Search Essentials, formerly called the Webmaster Guidelines.
Ask about expected results, timing, and how success will be measured.
Ask about experience in the client's industry.
Ask about experience in its country or city.
Ask about international-site experience.
Ask how long the SEO has been in business.
Ask how communication will work, whether all changes will be shared, and whether recommendations and reasoning will be explained in detail.
Business curiosity, references, audit access, and evaluation

A good SEO should ask what makes the business distinctive, who its competitors are, how Search can help, and how customers currently discover it. Lack of interest in the business is a reason to look elsewhere.
Check references for usefulness, ease of collaboration, and positive results.
For an initial audit, carefully understand the work and grant only read access to Search Console, not write access. The audit should provide realistic improvement estimates and estimated effort.
A first-place guarantee is a reason to reject a provider. Tools have no access to Google's internal ranking data and are not evaluated or endorsed by Google.

Before significant changes based on a tool audit, compare recommendations with official guidance and decide critically. Ask for supporting Google documentation, alignment of AI/AEO/GEO advice, and appropriate tools.
Every warning sign and the publisher's responsibility
Be skeptical of unsolicited SEO emails, including claims that a site is absent from many engines or directories.
No provider can guarantee number one, claim a privileged relationship that buys placement, or offer meaningful priority submission to Google.
Reject secrecy and unexplained changes. Ask for clear descriptions; deceptive content can remove a site from the index, and the site owner remains responsible for a hired company's actions.
If a provider has server/FTP access, it should explain all changes. Transparency matters for technical work as well as content.

You should not have to link to the SEO as a condition of service. Link-popularity schemes and submission to thousands of search engines are warning signs and typically do not create worthwhile results.
Unethical aggressive techniques can reduce visibility or lead to index removal under Google's spam policies.
Reporting issues and interview preparation

The page provides routes for reporting suspected deceptive services: the FTC for US complaints and econsumer.gov for complaints involving companies in other countries. These are source references, not a recommendation about a particular case.

Prepare honest examples from your five to six years of work. For each, explain the business problem, baseline, intervention, result, timeframe, and limitations. Those presentation elements are interview coaching, not a Google-mandated report format.
Do not invent success metrics, clients, or expertise. If a sector or country is new to you, explain the transferable process and how you would learn its constraints.

Things to consider when hiring an SEO

chapters.title: Google Search's guidance on using third-party SEO tools, services, and advice
chapters.takeaway: Tools can improve workflows, but their scores and predictions are not Google's internal ranking data. Evaluate claims against official guidance and use Search Console for first-party evidence.
notes: Verify advice and identify what kind of claim it is
The article covers external advice about SEO, listings, and AI experiences, including AEO and GEO.

Some advice is useful; some misrepresents what Google says or how its systems work. Good advice either identifies itself as an opinion based on data or experience, or supports a Google-specific claim with actual official documentation.

Compare proposed action with official SEO guidance and the generative AI guide, then make an informed site-specific decision. Citation quality matters: a link to Google is not proof that the cited page supports the exact claim.
All five example tool/service categories
Sitemap generation.
Indexing directives.
Content described as SEO-optimized.
Recommendations claiming to improve rankings of existing material.
AI-experience visibility tools marketed as AEO or GEO.
These categories are not automatically prohibited. Their value depends on the work they actually do and the truth of their claims.
Approval claims, internal-data claims, and guarantees
Google does not evaluate third-party SEO services. Claims that a product is accepted, approved, or endorsed by Google Search should be treated skeptically.
No third-party SEO tool has access to Google's internal ranking data. A vendor's score or prediction comes from the vendor, not from Google's ranking system.
Using a tool does not guarantee ranking success. Predictions can fail. Distinguish a useful estimate from a known Google fact.
Google strongly encourages Search Console, whether or not other tools are used, because it provides key information directly from Google Search.
Practical evaluation framework (interview application)
State the claim precisely, inspect its supporting source, and separate an observed tool metric from a proposed cause of ranking changes.
Confirm the issue on actual pages or in first-party evidence. Estimate user benefit and implementation cost, then prioritize by the business need.
Test reasonable hypotheses when appropriate and explain limitations. Third-party research can be informative even when it is not an official rule; label it honestly.
The guide does not state that every non-Google observation is worthless. It asks for critical evaluation and does not authorize vendors to present their own metrics as Google's.

headings.text: Evaluate and verify external SEO advice against official Google guidelines
Think critically about using third-party SEO tools and services

chapters.title: Overview of crawling and indexing topics
notes: This is a navigation overview, not a detailed technical specification. It explains the scope: controlling how Google finds and parses content, and preventing unwanted crawling.
Its topic map includes file types, URL structure, sitemaps, recrawl requests, faceted navigation, crawl budget, HTTP/network/DNS errors, and Google crawlers.
Other areas are robots.txt, canonicalization, mobile sites, AMP, JavaScript, valid metadata, robots directives, crawlable links, and outbound-link qualifications.
Removal topics distinguish controlling sharing, removing pages and images, and safely redacting information.
Site-change topics include redirects, migrations, A/B tests, and temporary closures. Detailed claims must come from the corresponding specialist page.

chapters.title: File types indexable by Google
notes: Google can index most text-based files and certain encoded document formats. Content-Type is the principal type signal; extensions or reparsing can help when the header is missing or wrong.
Flat formats listed: CSV; KML/KMZ; GPX; HTML; SVG; TeX/LaTeX; plain text and common programming-language source code; WML/WAP; and XML.
Encoded formats listed: PDF, PostScript, EPUB, HWP, Excel, PowerPoint, Word, OpenOffice presentations/spreadsheets/text, and RTF. The full extensions are in the source reference.
Image formats listed: BMP, GIF, JPEG, PNG, WebP, SVG, AVIF. Video formats include MP4, MOV, WebM and the complete longer list in the reference.
The list describes supported types, not a promise that every accessible file will be indexed.
filetype: restricts a search by file type or extension; the page's example searches RTF files containing a specified term.

chapters.title: URL structure best practices for Google Search
notes: Crawlable URLs follow IETF STD 66. Reserved characters must be percent encoded; non-ASCII characters should be percent encoded in link href values as documented.
Do not use fragments such as #/products to load distinct content; use the History API for JavaScript routing.
Use standard parameter encoding: = between a key and value, & between parameters; multiple values can use a compatible separator such as a comma.
Make URLs intelligible: descriptive readable words, the audience's language or transliteration, and hyphens rather than underscores for word separation.
Remove unnecessary parameters that do not change the content. Google treats differently cased URLs as distinct; normalize consistently when the server treats them as equivalent.
Multiregional examples include country-code domains and locale subdirectories.
URL explosions can arise from additive facets, irrelevant referral/sort parameters, session IDs, infinite calendars, and broken relative links.
Prefer cookies to session IDs in URLs where possible. The source suggests nofollow for links to unrestricted future calendar pages and root-relative URLs to avoid broken parent-relative expansions.
For problematic dynamic/search/calendar/filter spaces, appropriate robots.txt blocks may control crawling. They are not a substitute for noindex when index exclusion is the objective.

headings.text: Requirements for a crawlable URL structure
Don't use URL fragments to change content
Use a common encoding for URL parameters
Make it easy to understand your URL structure
Use as few parameters as you can
Be aware that URLs are case sensitive
Avoid common issues related to URLs
Additive filtering of a set of items

chapters.title: Link best practices for Google
notes: A reliably crawlable link is an a element with an href that resolves to an actual web address. Script-event-only elements or anchors without href are unreliable.
JavaScript-inserted links can be crawlable if their resulting markup meets the same requirements.
Put visible descriptive anchor text inside the anchor. An empty anchor may fall back to its title attribute; an image link uses the image's alt attribute.
Test JavaScript-inserted anchor text in rendered HTML with URL Inspection.
Good text is descriptive, reasonably concise, and relevant to both context and destination. Avoid generic labels, unwieldy phrases, forced keywords, and chains of adjacent links.
Surrounding words also provide context. Read anchor text alone to check whether it communicates the destination.
Every important page should be linked from at least one other page on the site; there is no magical ideal count of links per page.
Trusted external citations can help readers and credibility. Do not add nofollow to every external link. Qualify paid and user-generated links appropriately.

headings.text: Internal links: cross-reference your own content
External links: link to other sites

chapters.title: Learn about sitemaps
notes: A sitemap describes important pages/files and their relationships, helping efficient crawling. It can contain modification dates, language alternates, and image/video/news information.
Proper internal linking may allow Google to discover most content without a sitemap; a sitemap can still help large, complex, new, or media-heavy sites.
Strong use cases: large inventories, few external links to a new site, rich media, or Google News content.
It may be less necessary for a comprehensively linked site of about 500 important search pages or fewer, with little media or news requiring discovery.
CMS software may already generate a sitemap. Check the platform rather than assume a new manual file is needed.
Discovery support does not guarantee that every listed URL will be crawled or indexed.

chapters.title: Build and submit a sitemap
notes: Supported formats are XML; RSS/mRSS/Atom 1.0; and text. Google has no preferred format. XML can express the broadest extensions; feeds usually cover recent URLs; text is a simple URL list.
A single sitemap is limited to 50 MB uncompressed or 50,000 URLs. Split larger inventories and optionally use an index.
Use UTF-8 and fully qualified absolute URLs. Unless submitted through Search Console, location limits scope to descendants of the parent directory; root placement is recommended.
Include preferred canonical URLs, rather than every duplicate. Annotate separate desktop/mobile versions correctly if both are listed.
XML values need entity escaping. Google ignores priority and changefreq. Accurate lastmod should reflect significant changes, not a copyright-date-only edit.
RSS 2.0 and Atom 1.0 are accepted; mRSS can convey video. Text files must contain one URL per line, no other content, and a .txt extension.
CMS generation is often available. Manual creation suits a few dozen URLs; larger files should be generated from reliable website data. URL ordering does not matter to Google.
Submission is a hint, not a guarantee of downloading or use. Submit through the Sitemaps report/API, declare in robots.txt, or use WebSub for RSS/Atom updates.

Cross-site submission through Search Console requires verified ownership of all included sites. With robots.txt, prepare a separate sitemap per site and reference it from that site's robots.txt even if hosted centrally.
Use the Sitemaps report and linked troubleshooting documentation for processing errors. The full format examples and cross-site examples are preserved in the reference.

headings.text: Additional notes about RSS, mRSS, and Atom 1.0
Additional notes for text file sitemaps
Let your CMS generate a sitemap for you
Automatically generate a sitemap with tools
How to cross-submit sitemaps for multiple sites

chapters.title: Manage your sitemaps with a sitemap index file
notes: Split oversized sitemaps so each child remains under the generic size/URL limits; an index lets you submit many child sitemaps together.
Index files follow the Sitemap Protocol and the general sitemap requirements.
Child files normally must be on the same site and in the same directory or lower than the index. Documented cross-site submission can waive the same-site requirement.
Required tags are sitemapindex, sitemap, and loc. An index can contain up to 50,000 loc entries; Search Console accepts up to 500 sitemap index files per site.
Optional lastmod describes when the child sitemap file changed, in W3C Datetime format. Do not confuse this with a page's lastmod inside an ordinary sitemap.
The reference retains the two-child XML example and links to submission, combined extensions, and troubleshooting.

chapters.title: Image sitemaps
notes: Image sitemaps help expose images Google might not otherwise find, including images reached with JavaScript. A separate image sitemap or extensions in an existing sitemap are equally acceptable.
Generic sitemap requirements and general image best practices still apply.
The image namespace is http://www.google.com/schemas/sitemap-image/1.1. Required tags are image:image and image:loc.
Each url entry can have up to 1,000 image:image entries. The enclosing ordinary loc identifies the page; image:loc identifies the image.
Images can be hosted on a different domain, such as a CDN, if both domains are verified in Search Console. Ensure robots.txt does not block intended image crawling.
Removed/deprecated tags listed: image:caption, image:geo_location, image:title, image:license. Do not teach them as current required tags.

chapters.title: News sitemaps
notes: News entries can extend an existing sitemap or live in a separate one; a separate news sitemap may simplify Search Console tracking.
Update the same sitemap as new articles appear; do not create a brand-new sitemap for each update. Google News crawls it as often as the rest of the site.
Include articles created within the last two days. Older URLs can be removed from the news sitemap or retained without their news:news metadata.
An empty sitemap after a quiet period can trigger an intentionality warning but does not itself cause problems for Search.
Each url may have one news:news entry; a sitemap can contain up to 1,000 news:news entries. Split if necessary.
Required child tags: news:publication containing name and language, publication_date, and title.
Publication name must match Google News without parenthetical additions. Language uses ISO 639, with zh-cn and zh-tw exceptions.
publication_date is the original publication timestamp, not the sitemap insertion time, in accepted W3C forms. title matches the article title without author, publication name, or date.

chapters.title: Video sitemaps and alternatives
notes: Google recommends video sitemaps and also supports mRSS. Video entries can be in a separate file or extensions within a normal sitemap.

Videos should relate to the host page's main content. Referenced files must be accessible without login, robots blocks, or firewall blocks; the page describes HTTP/FTP support, not streaming protocols.

Required information: video:video, thumbnail_loc, title, description, and at least content_loc or player_loc. Prefer content_loc where available for fetching the actual media; embedded-platform examples use player_loc.
Neither content_loc nor player_loc should be the host-page loc. HTML and Flash are not valid media files for content_loc. The related structured-data equivalents are contentUrl and embedUrl.
Description has a 2,048-character maximum. The title should match the visible video's title, with proper escaping or CDATA; description should match meaning without requiring word-for-word identity.

Optional fields: duration (1–28,800 seconds), expiration_date, rating (0–5), view_count, publication_date, family_friendly, restriction, platform, requires_subscription, uploader, live, and tag (up to 32 tags).
Country/platform restriction values affect Search presentation rather than prevent actual user access. allow and deny have opposite treatment of unlisted locations/platforms.
Uploader text allows up to 255 characters, and its optional info URL must share the host page's domain. Expiration excludes the video after the date; update it for recurring videos.
The guide lists deprecated video fields and attributes, including category, gallery_loc, player autoplay/allow_embed, price, and tvshow. Their presence in old examples elsewhere is not a requirement.
mRSS uses media:content with medium=video and either its url or media:player; required text/thumbnail fields are media:title (100-character maximum), media:description (2,048), and media:thumbnail.

Optional mRSS fields include dcterms:valid, media:restriction and media:price with the listed attributes. The full video/mRSS tables, examples, namespaces, and exceptions are preserved in the reference.

chapters.title: How to combine sitemap extensions
notes: A page may have several content types, such as a localized news article with images and video. Extensions can coexist in one sitemap entry.
Declare every used extension's namespace on urlset. Google lists image, news, video, and xhtml for hreflang.
Add each extension's valid tags to the appropriate url element, following that extension's own implementation requirements.
Extension order does not matter after loc. Combined metadata can make files significantly larger, so enforce the generic size limits.
The full source retains namespace values and the combined news/video/hreflang XML example.

chapters.title: Ask Google to recrawl your URLs
notes: A hosted platform may already notify search engines of new content. Check platform documentation.
You cannot request indexing for a URL you do not manage. Individual URL requests require owner or full-user access to the Search Console property.
Use URL Inspection for a small number of URLs; use a sitemap for many, especially new sites and migrations.
Individual submissions have a quota. Requesting the same URL repeatedly does not accelerate crawling.
Crawling can take days to weeks. A request never guarantees instant inclusion or inclusion at all; monitor progress with the available reports/inspection.

headings.text: Use the URL Inspection tool (just a few URLs)
Submit a sitemap (many URLs at once)

chapters.title: Troubleshoot Google Search crawling errors
notes: Follow the five-part diagnosis: availability, important uncrawled URLs, update freshness, efficiency, and overcrawling.
Crawl Stats and URL Inspection expose availability problems and Hostload exceeded warnings. Better availability removes a constraint; it does not automatically increase crawl demand.
Server logs identify whether a specific URL was crawled; crawl activity and index inclusion are different. The guide's timing examples are expectations, not service-level guarantees.
Help discovery with current sitemaps/lastmod and real links, including equivalent mobile links. Avoid repeated unchanged sitemap submissions and expecting immediate complete crawling.
Improve server response and rendering speed, avoid long redirect chains, and block only non-critical unwanted resources. Making low-value pages faster does not by itself encourage more crawling.
Conditional requests can support 304 for unchanged content and 200 with updated content. Not every crawler sends the same cache headers on every request.
Avoid waste from facets, sessions, duplicates, soft 404s, hacked/spam pages, infinite spaces, carts, and state-changing pages. Reuse shared resource URLs for caching.
Do not repeatedly rotate robots rules or sitemaps to redistribute budget. Hiding recrawls reallocates resources only under the documented serving-limit condition.
Soft 404 can mean an error-like or empty page with a success status, including missing JS or database resources. Inspect rendered content and status before deciding.
Removed with no replacement: 404/410. Genuine replacement: 301. Still valid: repair missing resources/rendering or the misleading error state. A friendly custom 404 must still return 404.

Emergency 503/429 responses are temporary only; sustained errors can reduce crawling and remove URLs. AdsBot pressure can stem from Dynamic Search Ad targets; this page describes a three-week recurrence.

headings.text: See if Googlebot is encountering availability issues on your site
See if any parts of your site are not crawled, but should be
See if updates are crawled quickly enough
Specify content changes with HTTP status codes
Hide URLs that you don't want in search results
The page and content are no longer available
The page or content is now somewhere else
