chapters.title: Overview of Google crawlers and fetchers (user agents)
notes: Distinguish common automatic crawlers, special-case product crawlers, and user-triggered fetchers. Common crawlers respect robots.txt for automatic crawls; other categories have product-specific behavior.
Google uses many machines and datacenters. Requests primarily originate in the US, but other countries may be used when US access is blocked. Do not diagnose bot identity from geography alone.

Supported protocols include HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2, with HTTP/1.1 as the default. HTTP/2 can reduce resource costs but provides no product-specific ranking boost. A 421 response is the documented HTTP/2 opt-out mechanism.
FTP/FTPS crawling is also supported by the infrastructure but rare. gzip, deflate, and Brotli support is advertised through Accept-Encoding.

The infrastructure's default fetch limit is 15 MB, while individual crawlers/types can override it. Googlebot's specific page gives 2 MB for ordinary files and 64 MB for PDFs; do not conflate these scopes.
HTTP caching supports ETag/If-None-Match and Last-Modified/If-Modified-Since. ETag takes precedence when both validators are present, and Google recommends it to avoid date-format issues.
The source recommends considering both headers for other clients, and notes that products may use caching differently. It gives a recommended Last-Modified date format and a max-age suggestion.
Identification signals are user-agent, source IP, and reverse DNS hostname. Verification details belong to the corresponding guide.

headings.text: Technical properties of Google's crawlers and fetchers

chapters.title: Googlebot
notes: Googlebot denotes Smartphone and Desktop web crawlers. Most Search indexing uses mobile content, so smartphone requests generally dominate.
Their user-agent headers distinguish them, but both obey the same robots product token; robots.txt cannot selectively target one of the two.
The page describes a typical average request frequency of no more than once every few seconds, with short bursts possible. It is a general description, not a per-server traffic guarantee.
Search Googlebot fetches the first 2 MB of supported ordinary files and 64 MB for PDFs, measured uncompressed. It forwards only the downloaded portion for indexing consideration.
CSS/JS references are separate fetches with their own applicable limit. Image/video bots can have different limits. Do not add all resources together into one 2 MB page quota.
For US source IPs the documented timezone is Pacific Time. The overview covers other infrastructure properties.
Use robots.txt for crawl prevention, noindex for index exclusion, authentication for private access. Hiding links cannot keep a site secret; referrers can reveal URLs.
Verify alleged Googlebot requests because user-agent headers can be spoofed; DNS and published IP ranges are the documented methods.

headings.text: Blocking Googlebot from visiting your site

chapters.title: Reduce the Google crawl rate
notes: Google automatically chooses crawl rates to discover content without overloading infrastructure.
Investigate recent access logs and hosting evidence first. Common sources of sudden load are facets/sorting, large calendars, and Dynamic Search Ad targets.
Emergency reduction can use 500, 503, or 429 responses for a few hours or at most about one to two days. Significant error volumes reduce crawling across the hostname, including successful URLs.
Rate increases again as errors subside. Keeping these codes on the same URLs for days can cause Search index loss and other product effects.
Tradeoffs include slower discovery, less current prices/availability, delayed removal, and possible advertising interruptions.
If server responses cannot be changed, submit the exceptional high-crawl report with the desired rate. Evaluation may take days; this is not a way to request an increased rate.

headings.text: Understand the cause of the sharp increase in crawling
Exceptional requests to reduce crawl rate

chapters.title: Verify requests from Google crawlers and fetchers
notes: The verification table distinguishes common crawlers, special-case crawlers, and user-triggered fetchers, with separate DNS masks and JSON IP lists.
User-triggered fetches ignore robots.txt because a user requested them; special-case requests may or may not obey it. Do not apply common-crawler rules to every category.
For manual verification: reverse lookup the source IP, validate the appropriate Google-controlled domain, forward lookup that hostname, and ensure it returns the original IP.
A reverse hostname alone is not the complete method. Check domain boundaries and use the category-specific masks shown in the reference.
For automated verification, match the source IP against Google's published CIDR ranges in the appropriate category's JSON file.
The page also links user-triggered agent ranges and a general Google IP list for other requests such as Apps Script. A generic cloud address is not automatically Search Googlebot.
The complete reference preserves example host commands and every DNS mask/list name.

chapters.title: Introduction to robots.txt
notes: robots.txt manages URL crawl access and traffic. It does not enforce privacy and is not reliable web-page/PDF index exclusion.
Google can index a disallowed URL using external information without fetching its content; the result may appear without a description.
Embedded media/resources on a blocked page may not be fetched through that page, but other crawlable references can expose them.
For image/video/audio media, blocking the actual file can prevent it appearing in Search, although links and direct user access remain possible.
Block unimportant resources only when their absence does not impair page understanding. Do not block critical scripts or CSS blindly.
Crawlers choose whether to follow robots instructions and can interpret syntax differently. Malicious crawlers need access restrictions rather than voluntary rules.
Use noindex with access allowed for index exclusion; use authentication for confidential material. Combining contradictory controls can defeat the intended result.
CMS platforms may expose visibility settings instead of editable robots.txt. The source links creation, update, and specification guides.

headings.text: What is a robots.txt file used for?
Understand the limitations of a robots.txt file
Create or update a robots.txt file

chapters.title: How Google interprets the robots.txt specification
notes: Google implements the Robots Exclusion Protocol with the documented exceptions for user-controlled fetches and safety crawling. The reference points to RFC 9309.

Place robots.txt at the site's root. Scope is host, protocol, and port; subdirectories and unrelated subdomains/protocols are not covered. Standard default ports are equivalent; nonstandard ports have separate scope.
2xx: parse the file. 3xx: follow at least five hops, then treat unresolved robots redirection as 404; logical JS/frame/meta redirects are not followed.
4xx other than 429: treat the file as absent, with no restrictions. 401/403 are not valid throttling tools. DNS/network failures are treated as server errors.

For robots 5xx failures: stop site crawling for the first 12 hours while retrying; then use the last good file for the next 30 days if available. Without cache, assume no restrictions. Later behavior depends on general site availability.
Cache generally lasts up to 24 hours, with exceptions and Cache-Control effects. The file must be UTF-8 plain text; content after 500 KiB is ignored.
Field names and user-agent matching are case-insensitive; allow/disallow path values are case-sensitive. Valid supported fields are user-agent, allow, disallow, sitemap. crawl-delay is not supported.
Empty allow/disallow paths are ignored. Comments start with #. Sitemap locations are absolute, can be cross-host, and are not bound to one user-agent group.
Most-specific matching user-agent group wins; group order is irrelevant. Multiple equally applicable specific groups merge, but the global * group is not merged into a specific group.
Sitemaps do not break groups for the rules parser. Multiple consecutive user-agent lines can define one group.
Raw UTF-8 and percent-encoded UTF-8 paths are compared in their encoded form. * matches zero or more characters; $ anchors the URL end.
Path matches are prefix-based and case-sensitive: /fish differs from /fish/ and /Fish. The full wildcard matching table is retained in the reference.
For conflicting path rules, use the most specific rule by path length; equal-specificity conflicts use the least restrictive rule. Do not assume the last-written rule wins.

headings.text: File location and range of validity
Handling of errors and HTTP status codes
Order of precedence for user agents
URL matching based on path values

chapters.title: What is canonicalization
notes: Canonicalization selects a representative URL from duplicate or very similar content; it is also called deduplication.
Common duplicate sources: regional same-language versions, mobile/desktop variants, HTTP/HTTPS, sorting/filtering, and accidentally public demo sites.
Some duplication is normal and not a spam violation, but many duplicate URLs can confuse users and fragment reporting.
Google identifies primary content, clusters similar pages, and selects the most complete/useful representative using collected signals.
Canonicals are crawled most regularly; alternates are crawled less frequently to reduce site load.
HTTPS, redirects, sitemap inclusion, and canonical annotations influence selection. A stated preference is a hint, not a command.
Genuine translated primary content is not duplicate just because the layout is shared; translating only headers/footers while retaining the same main language is different.
Same-language regional variants can use canonicalization and hreflang together. Results usually point to the canonical but can select a better-suited alternate.

headings.text: How Google indexes and chooses the canonical URL

chapters.title: How to specify a canonical URL with rel="canonical" and other methods
notes: Redirects and rel=canonical annotations are strong signals; sitemap inclusion is weak. Consistent methods can reinforce each other, but an explicit preference is not required for every site.
Benefits: preferred visible URLs, consolidated signals, simpler metrics, and less duplicate crawling.
Do not use robots.txt, the Removals tool, fragments, or noindex as canonicalization substitutes. Keep signals consistent and link internally to canonical URLs.
The current guide explicitly recommends a self-referential canonical on the canonical page. hreflang should point to an appropriate same-language canonical, with the documented substitute exception.
Prefer canonical in original HTML. If JavaScript must supply it, do not contradict or replace a different source-HTML canonical; avoid multiple conflicting declarations.
An HTML canonical belongs in a valid head. Absolute URLs are recommended even though relative paths are supported.
A Link HTTP response header can specify canonicals for supported non-HTML documents such as PDFs; this header method is supported for web search results only.
Do not add alternate-language/media/type attributes to the canonical annotation and assume they set canonicals; use proper alternate annotations for those relationships.
Prefer choosing either the HTML annotation or HTTP header instead of implementing both inconsistently. Sitemaps nominate preferred URLs but do not explicitly map duplicates to them.
Use permanent redirects when deprecating duplicate pages. All permanent methods have the same Search effect, but HTTP redirects are generally noticed most quickly.

HTTPS is usually preferred, but invalid certificates, insecure dependencies, HTTPS-to-HTTP redirects or HTTP canonical signals can override it. HSTS cannot repair conflicting certificate/redirect failures.
URLs in reciprocal hreflang clusters may be preferred to otherwise similar URLs outside the cluster. The complete implementation comparisons and examples are in the reference.

headings.text: Reasons to specify a canonical URL
Prefer HTTPS over HTTP for canonical URLs

chapters.title: Fix canonicalization issues
notes: Inspect the Google-selected canonical in URL Inspection, then consider whether it might actually be the better representative for users.
If the canonical is in a property you do not own, you cannot see the duplicate's traffic in that property's data.
Check CMS canonical/redirect errors, server host misconfigurations, missing localized annotations, hacked redirects or cross-domain canonicals, syndication, and external copies.
When distinct pages were incorrectly clustered, make their primary content clearly and significantly different. Purely cosmetic differentiation is not the advice.
The current guide says duplicate-cluster reassessment can take up to two weeks; clear content differences may separate faster. This is not a guaranteed resolution deadline for all cases.
Request indexing for the important corrected URLs within quota.
Canonical elements are not the recommended way to prevent syndication duplication; the source recommends partners block indexing when that is the objective.
Copyright removal and host contact are mentioned for unauthorized copies; retain them as source pointers, not legal advice about a specific dispute.

chapters.title: Mobile site and mobile-first indexing best practices
notes: Google uses smartphone-crawled mobile content for indexing and ranking. A separate mobile version is not required for inclusion, but mobile friendliness is strongly recommended.

Configurations: responsive design (same URL/HTML, adaptive display), dynamic serving (same URL, different HTML, user-agent/Vary handling), and separate URLs. Responsive design is recommended as easiest to implement and maintain.
Keep mobile resources crawlable, robots directives equivalent, and primary content available without click/swipe/type requirements.
Maintain equivalent content and meaningful headings. Tabs and accordions can save space while preserving content; removing mobile information can reduce what Google knows.
Keep structured data on both versions, with correct mobile URLs; the guide prioritizes Breadcrumb, Product, and VideoObject if necessary. Keep titles and descriptions equivalent.
Avoid disruptive mobile ads. Provide high-quality supported images, equivalent alt text/captions, and stable resource URLs. Different mobile image URLs can cause temporary image-traffic effects.
Videos need supported formats/tags, stable URLs, equivalent markup, and prominent placement.
For m-dot: match error states, do not collapse distinct desktop pages into one mobile homepage, avoid fragment routes, verify both properties, and allow sufficient host capacity.

Keep mobile hreflang links between mobile URLs and desktop hreflang links between desktop URLs. In the documented separate-URL setup, desktop remains canonical and mobile is its alternate, even with mobile-first indexing.

The full source contains every troubleshooting entry: missing markup/images/alt/title/description, noindex, blocked resources, low-quality images, error URLs, fragments, duplicates, mobile-home redirects, ads/content/video quality, and hostload.

headings.text: Make sure that Google can access and render your content
Make sure that content is the same on desktop and mobile
Put the same metadata on both versions of your site
Check the placement of your ads
Additional best practices for separate URLs
Mobile URL is an error page
Desktop site redirects to the mobile home page

chapters.title: Understand the JavaScript SEO basics
notes: JavaScript processing has crawl, render, and index phases. Google checks robots access first, extracts links from initial HTML, and later from rendered HTML.
The guide says 200 responses queue for rendering unless noindex rules prevent it; non-200 responses may skip rendering. Queue time varies, not a fixed delay.
Server-side/prerendered content remains useful for performance and clients that do not execute JavaScript.
JavaScript can set titles/descriptions and canonicals, but avoid changing a different source canonical or creating conflicting multiple canonicals. Prefer original HTML where feasible.
Use compatible code, feature detection, and appropriate polyfills/fallbacks. Meaningful HTTP status codes communicate missing, restricted, and moved content.
SPAs should not return indexable successful-looking error pages: redirect to a real server 404 URL or add noindex for the error state.
Use real a href links and History API routes rather than fragments for distinct views.
Do not expect JavaScript to remove an initial noindex: Google may skip the rendering required to do so.
Googlebot/WRS caching can retain old CSS/JS despite cache headers; content-fingerprinted filenames solve version ambiguity.
JavaScript can inject JSON-LD; test it. Web components are supported by flattening light/shadow DOM, with slot projection where needed. Check actual rendered HTML for meaningful content.
The full reference preserves examples for SPA routing, API errors, canonical injection, robots rules, and web components.

headings.text: Describe your page with unique titles and snippets
Avoid soft 404 errors in single-page apps
Use the History API instead of fragments
Properly inject the rel="canonical" link tag
Follow best practices for web components

chapters.title: Fix Search-related JavaScript problems
notes: WRS may not fetch analytics/reporting resources that do not contribute to main content; client analytics is not a complete measure of crawler activity.

Use Rich Results Test or URL Inspection to inspect resources, console errors, exceptions, and rendered DOM. Collecting user/Googlebot JS errors can help, but some parse errors are not caught by the example global handler.
Prevent SPA soft 404s with a real-404 destination or noindex error state. Do not assume browser routing produces meaningful server status codes.
Googlebot declines user-permission requests. Provide access without mandatory camera or similar permissions.
Avoid fragments for views; the AJAX crawling scheme has been deprecated since 2015. Use History API routing.
WRS does not preserve cookies, local storage, or session storage across page loads. Each directly requested URL must work without prior browsing state.
Fingerprint resources to avoid stale caches. Use feature detection and fallback for unavailable APIs such as WebGL.
Content retrieval needs HTTP; Googlebot does not support WebSockets/WebRTC connections. Provide HTTP fallback and robust handling.
Check component flattening and slot projection in rendered HTML. For JS paywalls, do not deliver full content then merely hide it if access protection is intended.
Retest after fixes and use the official help community for unresolved rendering problems.

chapters.title: Fix lazy-loaded content
notes: Lazy loading can improve performance but must not hide relevant content from crawlers.
Load when content is visible in the viewport, using native image/iframe lazy loading, IntersectionObserver with suitable fallback, or a compatible library.
Do not depend on clicks or scroll events as the necessary trigger; Google Search does not interact with the page. Avoid lazy-loading immediately visible content where it delays display.
Infinite-scroll chunks need persistent unique URLs with stable content, such as fixed page numbers rather than date=yesterday.
Link chunks sequentially for discovery. Update the visible URL with History API when the new chunk becomes primary.
Test rendered HTML in URL Inspection. Actual image/video src URLs should be present in the rendered output.

headings.text: Load content when it's visible in the viewport
Support paginated loading for infinite scroll

chapters.title: Dynamic rendering as a workaround
notes: Dynamic rendering is a workaround, not a recommended long-term solution. Google recommends server-side rendering, static rendering, or hydration instead.
It detects crawlers with JS problems, routes them to a rendering server, and provides a suitable version while other clients receive the usual client-rendered output.
Historically relevant cases include rapidly changing public JS content or unsupported features; not every site needs it.
It adds complexity and resource requirements, and can be enabled per page or across the site.
Similar content across human and crawler output is generally not cloaking. Completely different content can be cloaking; temporary setup errors are treated as ordinary errors.

headings.text: Sites that might use dynamic rendering

chapters.title: Use valid HTML to specify page metadata
notes: Valid HTML helps Google use metadata as documented. Google can understand some invalid HTML, but that does not make broken metadata harmless.
Metadata belongs in head, whose permitted elements are title, meta, link, script, style, base, noscript, and template.
img and iframe are common invalid head elements. Once one appears, Google assumes head ended and stops reading later metadata.
The source strongly advises removing invalid elements; if unavoidable, place them after metadata Google should see. Do not interpret tolerance of general malformed HTML as reliable head parsing.

headings.text: Use valid elements in the <head> element
Don't use invalid elements in the <head> element

chapters.title: meta tags and attributes that Google supports
notes: Meta tags provide page information to engines and clients; unsupported tags are ignored. Put them in a valid head and inspect through URL Inspection.
Supported tags listed: description; robots/googlebot; notranslate; nopagereadaloud; google-site-verification; Content-Type/charset; refresh; viewport; adult rating.
Description can be used for snippets in some situations. Robots defaults are index/follow and need not be declared; conflicting instructions use the more restrictive rule.
google-site-verification values must match the supplied case exactly. Other meta naming/content is generally case-insensitive as documented; semantic values still must be correct.
UTF-8 is recommended. Quote the Content-Type content value properly to avoid parsing problems.
notranslate disables translated Search presentation; nopagereadaloud addresses Google text-to-speech services. Adult rating supports SafeSearch.
Server-side 301 redirects are recommended over refresh redirects. Viewport communicates mobile rendering information.
Relevant HTML attributes include src, href, rel qualifications and data-nosnippet on div/span/section. Language recognition is based on textual content rather than relying on lang annotations.
Unsupported: meta keywords, HTML lang as a Search language signal, next/prev link values, and nositelinkssearchbox. The underlying user-facing HTML purposes of attributes are not negated.
JS changes to metadata should be avoided where possible and thoroughly tested when necessary. The source's complete supported-tag table and examples are retained.

chapters.title: Robots meta tag, data-nosnippet , and X-Robots-Tag specifications
notes: Page-level controls use robots meta tags or X-Robots-Tag headers; text-level exclusions use data-nosnippet. Google must be allowed to access the resource to read them.
robots applies broadly to crawlers; googlebot and googlebot-news are the Search-specific supported meta tokens. The guide discusses separate handling of non-search clients.
Place meta in head as best practice, although the spec says Google also respects body robots meta. Headers are suitable for non-HTML documents and can be user-agent qualified.
Conflicts choose the more restrictive result. Separate applicable tags can combine negative instructions rather than cancel them.
Valid rules listed: all, noindex, nofollow, none, nosnippet, indexifembedded, max-snippet, max-image-preview, max-video-preview, notranslate, noimageindex, unavailable_after.
nosnippet suppresses text/video previews, not necessarily static thumbnails. Its documented scope includes preventing direct-content input to AI Overviews/Mode.

max-snippet uses characters (0 means no snippet; -1 leaves length to Google). max-image-preview uses none/standard/large. max-video-preview uses seconds (0 permits at most a static image; -1 no limit).
indexifembedded only operates with noindex and permits embedded use. unavailable_after sets a valid timestamp and substantially reduces crawl rate after expiration.
Historical ignored rules: noarchive, nocache, nositelinkssearchbox. Do not rely on vanished cached-link or search-box features.

data-nosnippet is a boolean on span/div/section; even a value of false still activates it. Use valid closed tags; avoid JS toggling existing nodes because extraction can occur before or after rendering.

Structured data remains usable within a data-nosnippet element. Preview controls do not generally replace management of separately supplied schema data; the source identifies description-related exceptions and permissions.
Apache/NGINX examples show global/file-specific X-Robots headers for PDFs and images. Do not block crawling if those headers must be read.

headings.text: Reference of historical and other unused rules
Handling combined indexing and serving rules
Combining robots.txt rules with indexing and serving rules

chapters.title: Block Search indexing with noindex
notes: noindex can be delivered through an HTML meta tag or HTTP response header; both have the same effect for Google when fetched.
It removes the page from Search regardless of incoming links after Google processes it. It does not prevent direct user access.
Crawl access is essential: robots.txt blocks or other access failures can prevent seeing the rule. noindex in robots.txt is unsupported.
robots targets supporting search engines; googlebot limits the meta instruction to Google web crawlers. Other engines can interpret instructions differently.
X-Robots-Tag can express noindex or none and is useful for PDFs, images, and videos.
A page may persist until it is recrawled; revisit time can be months depending on importance. URL Inspection can request a recrawl, and urgent cases use the removal procedure.
Debug access/robots, the actual HTML or response seen by Googlebot, and Page Indexing's extracted noindex cases.

chapters.title: Qualify your outbound links to Google
notes: Normal editorial links need no qualification solely because they are external.
sponsored identifies advertisements and paid placements; nofollow remains acceptable for those links but sponsored is preferred.
ugc is recommended for forum/comment user contributions. The guide allows removing it for consistently trusted contributors as an editorial choice.
nofollow applies when other values do not fit and you do not want association or following from your site.
Multiple values can be space- or comma-separated. These link attributes generally discourage following but do not prevent discovery through other routes.
Use appropriate robots disallow to prevent your own URL being crawled; allow crawling and use noindex to prevent indexing. Link qualifiers are not privacy or universal index controls.

chapters.title: Control what you share with Google
notes: Reasons to limit exposure include confidential/restricted data, low-value or spam user material, and unnecessary duplicate crawling on large sites.
Remove content if it should not be public. Password protection restricts actual access to confidential material.
noindex suppresses Search appearance while leaving content accessible through links or direct requests.
For images and videos, robots disallow can prevent indexing by blocking file fetching; this is not the same behavior as web-page URL exclusion.
The page links opt-outs for selected Google products, such as Shopping, Hotels, and rentals, which differ from removing all Search presence.
For already visible material, follow the page-removal procedure. Ensure metadata and supposedly redacted content are genuinely removed.

headings.text: Remove the content from your site

chapters.title: Remove a page hosted on your site from Google
notes: For quick removal of an owned page, use the Removals tool; the guide describes removal within a day. Cover every URL variation that exposes the content.
Tool requests last about six months. Permanent exclusion additionally requires removing/updating the content, restricting access, or implementing crawlable noindex.
robots.txt is not the method for permanently removing a web page from Search.
A noindex page can remain accessible to users and to engines that ignore it; remove the content or protect access when confidentiality matters.
Other Google products have separate procedures for business details, knowledge panels, Shopping and related surfaces. For a page you do not own, use the relevant personal-information help route.

headings.text: Remove an image from search results
Remove information from other Google properties
How do I remove content from a site that I don't own?

chapters.title: Remove images hosted on your site from search results
notes: Urgent image removal uses the Removals tool, with a permanent measure as well to prevent reappearance after expiry.

Non-emergency methods are blocking the actual image with robots.txt or providing noindex in its X-Robots-Tag. They have the same documented removal effect, but headers require crawling; combining them is counterproductive.
Apply robots.txt on the image-host domain, including any CDN host. The guide gives single-image, repeated-rule, wildcard, all-image, and file-extension examples.
Googlebot-Image targets Google Images; the source says Googlebot excludes from all Google searches. Verify the actual objective and relevant client.
With a noindex image header, permit fetching. A page-level noimageindex does not stop another page exposing the same image; a header on the image addresses that file wherever embedded.
If the image host or CMS cannot provide these controls, deleting the hosted image may be needed. Images on sites you do not control use different help routes.

headings.text: Remove images with the noindex X-Robots-Tag HTTP header
How do I remove images from properties that I don't own?

chapters.title: Keep redacted information out of Google Search
notes: Visual concealment is not complete redaction: tiny text, matching background colors, overlays, history, uncropped originals, metadata, OCR and assistive technologies can reveal it.
Redact images before embedding them in documents. Crop/remove unwanted areas, remove undesired metadata, and export flattened non-vector formats such as PNG/WebP.
Delete unwanted text before publishing in a format that does not retain previous history. Use actual redaction tools rather than black rectangles placed over live text.
Review the exported public file's metadata and format-specific redaction behavior; conversion alone may preserve sensitive information.
Avoid sensitive names/emails in URLs or filenames. Use hashes in parameters instead, and consider authentication with an appropriately noindexed login page.
Verify the site in Search Console so urgent removal can be requested when necessary.

If exposed: remove the live original, request removal, host the genuinely redacted version at a different URL, update links, and seek removal of copies from other hosts. The guide references the Outdated Content tool as another update path.
Temporary Search removal and actual public-data removal remain separate tasks; the complete source's steps are preserved.

headings.text: Edit and export images before embedding them
Edit or remove unwanted text before moving to a public file format
What to do if unredacted or improperly redacted documents are indexed in Search

chapters.title: Redirects and Google Search
notes: Redirects resolve an existing URL to a different location. Uses include domain moves, merging sites, selecting a preferred URL, and sending users from replaced content to its successor.
Permanent redirects signal the target as canonical; temporary redirects do not provide that same canonicalization signal. Other signals can still lead to target indexing.
Server-side redirects have the highest chance of correct interpretation. Use 301 or 308 for a permanent move and 302, 303 or 307 for a temporary one.

The guide shows PHP, Apache and NGINX implementations. In PHP, set redirect headers before sending output. Keep implementation syntax from the full source examples rather than memorizing flattened snippets.
A meta refresh or HTTP Refresh with zero delay is interpreted as permanent; a positive delay is temporary. The HTML meta refresh belongs in the head.
Use JavaScript location redirects only when server-side or meta refresh methods are unavailable. Google must render the page to detect them, and rendering failure can prevent detection.
A crypto redirect is explanatory text plus a link rather than a conventional automatic redirect. It is the weakest listed option and should not be relied on when alternatives exist.
An old URL may temporarily appear as an alternate name in results after a move, helping users recognize the destination. This can be normal and fades over time.

headings.text: meta refresh and its HTTP equivalent

chapters.title: Changing your hosting
notes: This guide covers a hosting, infrastructure or CDN change without changing user-visible URLs; a domain/path/protocol change needs the URL-migration guide.

Copy and test the new infrastructure. For a temporary hostname, prevent indexing during testing; test Googlebot access, including firewalls and denial-of-service protections, and keep verification working.
Lower DNS TTL, for example to a few hours, at least a week ahead so old entries expire sooner during the switch.
Check that Search Console verification methods continue to work on the new site and remove temporary crawl/index restrictions before the public move.
Update DNS to the new hosting provider. If content changes meanwhile, ensure the new infrastructure also has those updates.
Monitor old/new server logs, DNS resolution and Search Console. A temporary crawl-rate dip followed by an increase can be expected while Google assesses the new host.
Retire old hosting once its logs show no remaining traffic; the move is not complete merely because DNS was edited.

headings.text: Copy and test your new site
Check that Googlebot is able to access the new hosting infrastructure
Lower the TTL value for your DNS records
A note about Googlebot's crawl rate

chapters.title: How to move a site
notes: This process covers HTTP-to-HTTPS, domain changes, site merges, and URL-path restructuring. Plan the move, prepare the new site, map URLs, implement redirects, update links, and monitor both sites.

Change one major thing at a time, consider a low-traffic period, and expect temporary ranking fluctuations. Small/medium sites can move together; large sites may move in sections, with test sections not proving full-site outcomes.

The move is processed per URL, not with a fixed site-wide deadline. The guide gives a few weeks for most pages of a small/medium site, with larger sites taking longer. Permanent redirects do not cause PageRank loss by themselves.

Prepare content, assets, server capacity, valid TLS for HTTPS, analytics, and Search Console verification for relevant old/new properties. Check a purchased domain's manual actions and prior removal history and carry over applicable disavow settings.

Inventory old URLs from CMS, logs, analytics, sitemaps and link reports, including media and supporting resources. Map each useful old URL to its correct new counterpart; intentionally removed content should return 404 or 410 rather than an irrelevant destination.
New pages need consistent self-referencing canonicals, updated hreflang annotations and internal links, and a new sitemap. Remove temporary noindex/robots restrictions before launch.

Use direct permanent server-side 301/308 redirects. Avoid chains: the guide says Googlebot can follow up to 10 hops, but recommends direct destinations and short unavoidable chains, ideally no more than 3 and fewer than 5.
Do not redirect many unrelated URLs to the home page: this can confuse users and be treated as soft 404. A genuine consolidated replacement is different.

Use Change of Address where appropriate for a domain/subdomain move. It is not required for HTTP-to-HTTPS, www/non-www switches, or path-only changes. Verify and handle relevant old domain properties.
Retain redirects generally for at least one year; keeping them longer can help users. Update important external/profile/ad links as well as internal links.
Submit the new sitemap. The article also describes old/new sitemap comparisons for monitoring; it does not make retaining an old sitemap a permanent requirement.

Monitor clicks, impressions, indexed counts, crawler/user traffic, redirects and errors. Old-site traffic should decline as new-site traffic rises. Investigate forgotten noindex/robots rules, wrong destinations, crawl errors, inadequate capacity and stale sitemaps.

Legacy wording: the article still mentions a manual Search Console crawl-rate setting. That tool was retired on January 8, 2024; use the current reduce-crawl-rate guidance instead. The original wording is preserved in the reference and flagged rather than silently rewritten.

headings.text: General best practices for site moves
Create a mapping of old to new URLs
Update all URL details on the new site
Use Search Console to monitor traffic
Use other tools to monitor traffic

chapters.title: Minimize A/B testing impact in Google Search
notes: A/B tests compare two or more variations of a change; multivariate tests examine multiple changes and their combinations. Tests can use separate URLs or dynamically vary one URL.
Small layout, color, image placement or call-to-action variations may greatly affect users while having little or no effect on snippets or ranking.
Do not cloak: Googlebot and humans must not be deliberately sent fundamentally different test URL sets. Googlebot generally does not support cookies and may see the version accessible without them.
For test variants with separate URLs, point rel=canonical to the original. This expresses the duplicate/variant intent better than noindex and avoids unintended indexing effects.
Use temporary 302 redirects for experiment routing, rather than permanent 301. The guide also permits JavaScript-based test redirects.
Run a test only as long as needed for reliable conclusions, based on traffic/conversion data. Then deploy the chosen version and remove alternate URLs, scripts and markup promptly.
Prolonged experiments designed to deceive search engines can lead to action. The source is SEO guidance, not a statistical test-design tutorial.

headings.text: Run the experiment only as long as necessary

chapters.title: Temporarily pause or disable a website
notes: For a temporary inability to fulfill orders, keep the site accessible and limit functionality, such as disabling checkout. Let people still find product information, reviews and wishlists.

Explain delays or closure with a clear banner; data-nosnippet can exclude its text from snippets. Update Product availability, cancelled events, Local Business hours and Merchant Center availability as applicable.
Ask for recrawling of a few changed pages through Search Console; use sitemaps for larger sets. Do not remove out-of-stock products merely to express availability.
Completely disabling a site is an extreme measure with uncertain recovery. It can reduce public business information, affect Knowledge Panels and verification/report access, and make recovery harder.

For an urgent 1–2 day shutdown, the guide describes an informational 503 page. For longer closure, provide an indexable 200-status home-page placeholder rather than serving indefinite 503 responses everywhere.
If using 503, keep robots.txt valid and accessible, use Retry-After with a best-effort estimate, and provide a light static page with reopening information and contact guidance.

Returning 503 prevents Google's systems refreshing that page's titles, descriptions, metadata and structured data. Test actual HTTP responses rather than assuming the visible page communicates the status.
Do not use site-wide robots disallow, 403/404/410, noindex, or temporary removal as the routine closure strategy. Those controls can remove visibility that customers need.

The guide mentions crawl-rate reduction and resetting a setting, but the Search Console manual limiter was retired in 2024. Current reduction guidance should be used; reducing crawl rate can delay freshness.

Regional access needs care. This page emphasizes US-origin crawling; the newer crawler overview says Google may use other countries if needed. Do not assume that blocking the US guarantees all Google crawlers are blocked; test verified crawler access and favor limiting local functionality.

chapters.title: Overview of Search appearance topics
notes: This overview maps Search appearance topics: AI, business information, dates, favicons, featured snippets, paywalls, Discover, images, preferred sources, regional features, profiles, site names, sitelinks, snippets, titles, places, translations, video, visual elements and Web Stories.
It explains that structured data helps Google understand a page and can support richer displays; it is a topic directory rather than a complete eligibility specification.

Its feature list includes Article, Breadcrumb, Carousel, Course list, Dataset, Discussion forum, Education Q&A, Employer aggregate rating, Event, Image metadata, Job posting, Local business, Math solver, Movie carousel, Organization, Practice problem, Product and its listed commerce subfeatures, Profile page, Q&A, Recipe, Review snippet, Software app, Speakable, paywalled content, Vacation rental and Video.
The current list is different from older SEO checklists. Do not assume every schema.org type has a supported Google rich result; consult the current search gallery and feature guide.
Package tracking and structured-data carousels beta appear under the Early Adopters Program, which pilots features with limited organizations.

chapters.title: AI features and your website
notes: AI Overviews summarize complex topics with supporting links. AI Mode supports deeper exploration, reasoning and comparisons. They can use different models and produce different responses and links.
Query fan-out can issue related searches across subtopics and data sources; AI Overviews do not trigger for every query.
A supporting-link page must be indexed and eligible for a Search snippet, meeting ordinary Search technical requirements. Eligibility and compliance do not guarantee serving.

Existing SEO fundamentals apply: accessible crawling/CDNs, internal discovery, useful text, page experience, relevant images/video, visible-content-consistent markup and current business/merchant information.
No special AI schema, AI text file, or extra technical requirement is specified for these features.

The captured 2025 article says AI traffic is included in the Web Performance report. Newer Google documentation also provides a dedicated generative AI impressions report; the update note supplies the current context.

The page lists Googlebot access and nosnippet/data-nosnippet/max-snippet/noindex as Search controls; Google-Extended has a different training/grounding scope. Newer Search Console generative-AI controls are covered in the update note.
Diagnose preview controls in the HTML received by Googlebot and allow time for recrawling and processing; this page gives days to months, not a fixed deadline.
Evaluate conversion quality and engagement alongside visibility. Google's observed higher-quality AI clicks are not a guarantee for every site.
