chapters.title: Influence your byline dates in Google Search
notes: A byline date is Google's estimate of publication or significant update time and is displayed when useful. No single date signal is definitive and display is not guaranteed.
Show a prominent human-visible date, correctly labeled Published or Last updated.
Add datePublished/dateModified on a CreativeWork subtype such as Article, BlogPosting or VideoObject, following structured-data rules.
A date is required; time is optional. Including time and the correct timezone in markup improves precision, including daylight-saving handling.
Keep visible and structured dates/times consistent; visible time/timezone may be omitted even if markup supplies them.
Dates should describe the page's publication/update, not a future date or the date of an event discussed on the page. Event markup can describe the event separately.
If Google chooses the wrong date, reduce competing dates. Google News has additional linked guidance; code examples are preserved in the source reference.

headings.text: How to provide date information to Google
Best practices for influencing byline dates

chapters.title: Define a favicon to show in search results
notes: Organic Search favicon guidance differs from the separate Google Ads logo specifications.
Add a supported icon link to the home-page head. Supported rel values include icon, shortcut icon, apple-touch-icon and apple-touch-icon-precomposed.
The href may be relative or absolute and may point to a CDN. The home page must be crawlable by Googlebot and the icon by Googlebot-Image.
One favicon is supported per hostname: a domain and a subdomain can differ, but individual subdirectories cannot have separate Search favicons.
The current August 2026 rule is square 1:1, at least 8×8 px; Google recommends larger than 48×48 px for various surfaces. Do not repeat an older multiple-of-48 rule as the current requirement.
Current supported file formats are BMP, GIF, ICO, PNG, JPEG, PPM and TIFF; use this specific list rather than assuming the general image list applies.
Keep the favicon URL stable and imagery representative and appropriate. Inappropriate symbols may be replaced by a default icon.
Recrawl the home page after a change; processing may take days to weeks and appearance is not guaranteed. The feedback form supports system improvement, not guaranteed individual action.

headings.text: Submit feedback about favicons in search results

chapters.title: Featured snippets and your website
notes: Featured snippets reverse the ordinary result layout by placing the descriptive extract first and can also appear in People Also Ask.
There is no markup that designates a page as a featured snippet; Google's systems choose it for a query.
nosnippet blocks both ordinary and featured snippets. data-nosnippet excludes marked text from both; when both exist, nosnippet takes priority.
To retain ordinary snippets while discouraging featured snippets, experiment with shorter max-snippet values. Google supplies no universal minimum and low values do not guarantee exclusion.
Use nosnippet when guaranteed snippet exclusion is required, accepting its broader effect.
A featured-snippet click can scroll to the quoted section automatically. If browser support or precise section identification fails, the click goes to the top of the page.

headings.text: How can I opt out of featured snippets?
How can I mark my page as a featured snippet?
What happens when a user clicks a featured snippet?

chapters.title: Flexible Sampling general guidance
notes: Flexible Sampling covers subscription-content exposure and its effects on users, referrals and conversion. Experiment cautiously rather than treat one quota as universally optimal.
Metering allows a quota of full articles before a subscription/login barrier. Lead-in exposes part of an article without offering all of it.
The guide generally favors monthly over daily quotas for flexibility, concentrating barriers on engaged users while letting newcomers experience value.
For many daily news publishers it suggests 6–10 articles per user per month, with 10 as a starting experiment. These are recommendations, not universal ranking eligibility requirements.
Exposing the opening sentences after the meter is exhausted can help users understand value and encourage subscription.

Track referral/conversion effects and how often search visitors hit paywalls. The source reports satisfaction degrading above about 10% paywall views, roughly 3% of the audience exposed; treat this as its study observation, not a ranking threshold.
Advanced publishers can vary allowances for highly engaged users while preserving more access for others.

Mark paywalled content with suitable structured data so Google can distinguish it from cloaking. If content must not reach the browser, choose an implementation that does not deliver it merely to hide it client-side.

chapters.title: Discover and your website
notes: Discover recommends content by interests and Web/App Activity rather than requiring a keyword query. Indexed policy-compliant content is automatically eligible, with no special markup and no display guarantee.
Older content can appear if relevant and useful. Violations may generate Discover manual actions in Search Console.
Helpful people-first content, accurate non-clickbait headlines, timely stories or unique insights and good page experience are recommended.

Large images: at least 1,200 px wide, more than 300,000 total pixels, recommended 16:9 aspect ratio, and max-image-preview:large or AMP. Crop thoughtfully rather than distort or lose essential detail.
Use relevant representative schema.org images or og:image to influence the thumbnail; avoid generic logos and text-heavy imagery.
Interest feeds may not recommend forms, petitions, job applications, code repositories or satire without context; Discover also filters shocking/unexpected content beyond SafeSearch.
Treat Discover visits as supplemental and volatile. Interest changes, content mix and Search updates can affect traffic without proving a publishing-quality problem.
The Discover performance report covers clicks, impressions and CTR for up to 16 months when the impression threshold is met, including Chrome Discover surfaces.

headings.text: Why Discover traffic might change over time

chapters.title: Google image SEO best practices
notes: Images can surface in text results, Discover and Google Images; follow crawl/index eligibility as well as image-specific implementation requirements.
Use img src for discoverability, including inside picture. Google does not index CSS background images. Responsive srcset/picture implementations need an img src fallback.
Image sitemaps can list images on other domains; verify a CDN host in Search Console where possible and diagnose image access separately from page access.
Supported image formats: BMP, GIF, JPEG, PNG, WebP, SVG and AVIF. Match extensions to type. Base64 data URIs are possible but can significantly enlarge HTML.
Balance sharp high-quality images with optimized size and responsive delivery; use PageSpeed Insights and appropriate performance techniques.

Preferred previews can be influenced through primaryImageOfPage, image attached to the main entity, or og:image. Choice is automated, not guaranteed; use representative high-resolution non-logo images without extreme ratios or excessive text.

Landing-page titles, descriptions, captions, nearby relevant text and structured data help Google understand an image and its Search presentation. Follow each supported feature's image and markup requirements.
Filenames provide light clues: concise descriptive names beat generic camera IDs. Translate localized filenames with suitable URL encoding.
Helpful descriptive alt text supports accessibility and Google's understanding; avoid keyword stuffing. Image-link alt text can act as anchor text. Inline SVG accessibility can use a title element.
Reuse a consistent URL for an image across pages to permit caching and avoid unnecessary crawling.

To opt out of full-size Images inline linking, inspect the referrer and respond to Google-domain requests as documented with 200 or 204 and no content. Google can still show a crawl-time thumbnail; the guide says this is not image cloaking.
Full index exclusion is a different control. Label explicit content appropriately for SafeSearch, which can show, blur or block explicit results according to user settings.

headings.text: Help us discover and index your images
Use HTML image elements to embed images
Specify a preferred image with metadata
Check your page title and description
Use descriptive filenames, titles, and alt text
Opt out of Google Images inline linking

chapters.title: Establish your business details with Google
notes: Establish an official business presence through verified Business Profile and Search Console ownership; these verify different assets and serve different purposes.
Business Profile supports address, contact details, business type and photos in Maps and related business displays.
A verified official representative can request edits to a knowledge panel, while algorithms also collect public-web entity information.
Organization markup can identify the preferred logo; Breadcrumb markup clarifies site hierarchy. Structured data does not replace verification or guarantee a panel.
Make accurate customer-support contact routes available; the page links its dedicated best-practices guide.
Troubleshoot by testing markup, allowing roughly a week for processing after crawling, and suggesting corrections through the knowledge-panel feedback/edit routes.

headings.text: Register your website with Search Console
Update your site's Google knowledge panel

chapters.title: Top Places List
notes: Top Places List can show independent lists that mention a business with a physical location, such as restaurant recommendation lists.
A listing must be editorially curated, genuine, independent and unsponsored.
Automated data/metric templates and vulgar or offensive language fail the stated listing requirements.
Search appearance is illustrative, not guaranteed. Publishers can opt their lists out using the linked local/property opt-out mechanism.

headings.text: Prevent your website's lists from appearing in a Top Places List feature

chapters.title: Opt out of display on local search results and other Google properties
notes: Applies to Googlebot-fetched material in Shopping, Flights, Hotels/vacation rentals and specialized local results.
Existing displays are removed within 30 days.
Set it for a whole domain, including subdomains; other domains need separate settings. Individual paths or subdomains cannot be selected.
Local suppression is worldwide; the other listed properties are covered on google.com.
Manage the setting in Search Console. This is a property-specific display control.

chapters.title: Understanding page experience in Google Search results
notes: Assess page experience holistically: Core Web Vitals, secure delivery, mobile display, ad interference, intrusive overlays and clear distinction between main and secondary content.
The current September 2026 FAQ says there is no single page-experience signal; core ranking uses a variety of signals.

It explicitly says Core Web Vitals are used by ranking systems, while other page-experience aspects do not directly make a site rank higher. Those improvements still help users and align with desired experience.
A perfect score in a report or third-party tool is not a ranking guarantee or necessarily the best SEO use of time.
Evaluation is generally per page, with some site-wide assessments. Relevant content may rank despite poor experience; good experience can help when many useful answers compete.

Resources include the CWV report/guides, secure-connection checks, interstitial guidance, Lighthouse and experimental CrUX ad-count/density/weight metrics. The article still mentions an HTTPS report; use current Search Console availability rather than assuming every historic report persists.

headings.text: Is there a single "page experience signal" that Google Search uses for ranking?
What aspects of page experience are used in ranking?
Is page experience evaluated on a site-wide or page-specific basis?
How important is page experience to ranking success?

chapters.title: Avoid intrusive interstitials and dialogs
notes: Full-page interstitials and partial-page dialogs can obstruct content, frustrate users and impede search-engine understanding.
Use small banners for promotional notices, newsletter prompts or app installation instead of blocking the whole screen. Browser-native or standard HTML banners are examples.
Common maintained CMS libraries can distribute improvements, but their use does not by itself guarantee compliance.
Avoid covering the whole page or sending visitors to a separate page for consent/input unless legally required.
Legally mandatory gates are exempt from these general guidelines; where possible overlay the original content rather than redirect all URLs to one gate page.
Redirecting every incoming URL to a single consent page can leave only that page fetchable and present in Search.
For mandatory adult age gates, the guide recommends permitting verified Googlebot access without triggering the gate; verify requests rather than trust a spoofable user-agent.

chapters.title: Understanding Core Web Vitals and Google search results
notes: Core Web Vitals measure real-world loading, responsiveness and visual stability: LCP, INP and CLS respectively.
The Search page recommends LCP within 2.5 seconds, INP below 200 ms and CLS below 0.1. The linked Web Vitals guide defines good thresholds as LCP ≤2.5 s, INP ≤200 ms and CLS ≤0.1.
Google's measurement guide evaluates the 75th percentile separately for mobile and desktop; passing requires all three good metrics. This detail comes from the linked supplementary Web Vitals source.
Use the Search Console CWV report and appropriate measurement/debugging tools. Lab diagnostics and real-user field measurements have different purposes and should not be treated as identical.
Good metrics support users and Search, but the page-experience FAQ explicitly rejects a guaranteed top ranking or a perfect-score-only SEO strategy.
Full optimization instructions for each metric are linked resources, not invented prescriptions in this short overview.

chapters.title: Help your readers find your site through preferred sources in Google Search
notes: Users can select a publication as a preferred source, making its content more likely in Top Stories and enabling a preferred badge. AI Mode/Overviews can also highlight it for users who selected it.
Current availability is global for Top Stories in Search-supported languages, and for AI features in their supported locales/languages.
Sites must be included in Search generative AI features in Search Console to qualify for the described displays. Domain/subdomain sites qualify; individual subdirectories do not.
Check whether the publication appears in the source-preferences tool. Publisher promotion methods help readers opt in but are not mandatory eligibility markup.
Recommended standard implementation loads Google's publisher.js library and adds a google-add-preferred-source-btn div; Google localizes and styles the button and returns readers to their page.
Optional data-theme sets light/dark; data-lang overrides the default browser-derived language.

Advanced SDK integration supports equivalent ES Module and standard script/IIFE capabilities with init and addPreferredSource. For manual script control, use preferred-sources-control=manual and the PREFERRED_SOURCE callback queue.
Without JavaScript, link to the source-preferences deeplink with the publication domain in q; text/image links can also be promoted in newsletters or social posts.
Custom or downloaded official badge assets are possible. This is user choice and personalization, not a publisher-controlled general ranking guarantee.

headings.text: How to help users find your site as a preferred source
Advanced JavaScript implementation with custom design assets

chapters.title: A guide to Google Search ranking systems
notes: Ranking is primarily page-level, using many signals and systems. Site-wide classifiers also contribute; strong or weak site-wide signals do not force every page to perform identically.
BERT helps understand word combinations and intent; neural matching relates query/page concepts; RankBrain relates words to concepts even without exact-term overlap.
MUM understands and generates language but is not described as a general Search ranking system here; it is used for specified applications such as vaccine information and featured-snippet callouts.

Crisis systems surface personal-crisis resources and SOS authority information during disasters. Reliable-information systems elevate authoritative sources/journalism and may display uncertainty/content advisories.
Deduplication reduces similar listings. A page promoted to a featured snippet is not repeated as an ordinary listing later on the first results page.
Exact-match-domain handling prevents query-matching domain words receiving too much credit. Freshness systems respond to query need, not a universal preference for recently edited pages.
Link analysis and evolved PageRank remain part of core ranking; local-news systems identify useful local sources.
Original-content systems help surface original reporting/content over copies or mere citations. Canonical annotations can assist primary-page understanding for duplicated versions.

Removal-based demotions can arise from substantial legal or personal-information removal patterns. These are documented mechanisms, not a diagnosis that any individual ranking loss proves legal wrongdoing.
Passage ranking helps understand sections of a page's relevance; the guide does not describe a separately controlled passage index.
The reviews system seeks insightful expert/enthusiast analysis and original research. Spam detection, including SpamBrain, targets content/behaviors violating spam policies.
Site diversity generally limits one site's top listings to two, but relevant exceptions exist. Subdomains usually count with the root, with exceptions.

Historical systems: helpful content became part of core ranking in March 2024; Hummingbird marks a 2013 major improvement; Panda joined core in 2015 and Penguin in 2016. Do not present them all as standalone current updates.

chapters.title: Google Search's reviews system and your website
notes: The reviews system rewards substantial insightful analysis and original research by knowledgeable experts/enthusiasts, rather than thin summaries.
It covers first-party standalone recommendation/opinion/analysis content, not customer reviews posted in a product or service review section.
Eligible subjects include products, media, services and businesses; formats include single reviews, comparisons and ranked recommendations.
Evaluation is primarily page-level, but sites with substantial review content may receive wider evaluation. It improves regularly and continuously.
The documented language list is English, Spanish, German, French, Italian, Vietnamese, Indonesian, Russian, Dutch, Portuguese and Polish, globally.
Product structured data can help identify a product review, but the system does not solely depend on markup.

Improvements may support recovery over time, but review assessment is only one ranking factor and results can change for other reasons. The linked high-quality-review guide supplies further content advice.

headings.text: What does this system mean for my site?

chapters.title: Google Search's core updates and your website
notes: Core updates are broad improvements to systems serving helpful reliable results; they do not target individual sites or specific pages as a penalty.
Verify rollout completion and dates in the Search Status Dashboard before attributing a traffic change to an update.
Wait at least a full week after completion, then compare that period with a week before rollout began. Inspect affected pages/queries and separate Web, Images, Video and News patterns.
A small positional change such as 2 to 4 does not justify drastic alteration. A sustained large change such as 4 to 29 calls for deeper objective assessment.
Review the whole site's helpfulness and the most affected pages; independent unaffiliated feedback can reduce bias.
Avoid rumor-driven quick fixes. Improve content meaningfully for readers through better substance, organization and navigation.
Deleting is a last resort for unsalvageable material; removal of search-first sections can be considered when they cannot be improved.
Effects can take days or months and may or may not wait for another major update. Smaller unannounced updates also occur; there is no guaranteed recovery or fixed ranking position.

headings.text: Check if there's a traffic drop in Search Console
Assessing a large drop in position
Things to keep in mind when making changes
How long does it take to see an effect in Search results

chapters.title: Google Search spam updates and your site
notes: Automated spam detection operates continuously; announced spam updates are notable improvements to those systems.
SpamBrain is an AI-based prevention system that is improved to identify new spam patterns.
Sites affected should assess compliance with the actual spam policies, not assume a generic content rewrite addresses every spam mechanism.
Policy violations may reduce ranking or remove Search presence. Systems may learn improved compliance over months.
When link-spam benefits are neutralized, the old benefits cannot be regained by merely cleaning up; compliant improvement is not a promise to restore artificial link-driven positions.

chapters.title: Regional differences in Search experience
notes: This directory routes regional Search features by business region and query category; it does not describe globally identical Search displays.
EEA aggregator and supplier units cover hotels, flights, ground transportation, local businesses and products.
The EEA ecosystem carousel covers finance, weather, sports and translation. EEA job-site features cover job searches.
Places-site carousel/refinement features in the current directory apply to Türkiye local-business and hotel queries.
South African badge/refinement features target the specified local platforms and travel/commerce categories.
Structured-data host carousels are region/category-specific across EEA, Türkiye and South Africa; the dedicated beta page contains exact requirements and query lists.
A refinement chip, multi-provider aggregator unit and a single-site structured-data carousel are distinct experiences with different participation requirements.

chapters.title: Aggregator unit in Google Search
notes: The aggregator unit is a multi-provider experience for approved VSSs such as OTAs, metasearch services, comparison-shopping providers and directories.
For a relevant query, the top-ranked provider is expanded by default; users can switch eligible providers, and only one aggregator unit is expanded at a time. Clicks lead to that provider's website.
The documented user market is EEA, for hotels, flights, long-distance trains/buses, products and local businesses; the supplier unit can appear alongside it.

Participation requires approved VSS status, relevant content, required data, quality standards and Search content-policy compliance. Express interest using the appropriate form; product/CSS contact routes differ from other categories.
Flights and transport use real-time APIs; lodging and local businesses use direct feeds. The source links each category's exact feed/API documentation.
Provide meaningful entity descriptions, images, verified ratings/counts, precise categories, amenities and hours where relevant.
Use factual descriptive titles; avoid promotional words, ALL CAPS, excessive punctuation or emoji. Prefer clear high-resolution original images without watermarks or promotional badges.
Keep prices and availability consistent with landing pages, refresh feeds and remove expired/out-of-stock listings. Use Search Console to monitor overall Search performance.

chapters.title: Supplier unit in Google Search
notes: The supplier unit gives visibility to direct providers such as hotels, airlines, shops and service providers, alongside the aggregator unit.
It appears only when the aggregator unit appears, for the documented EEA categories.
The site must serve EEA users and represent a relevant direct provider.
Additional data beyond web-crawl-accessible information is not required; optional feeds can enhance supplier results. Do not confuse its requirements with the aggregator's mandatory integrations.

headings.text: How to participate in the supplier unit

chapters.title: Ecosystem carousel in Google Search
notes: The ecosystem carousel offers alternative sources for queries benefiting from interactive data or visualization: finance, weather, sports and translation.
It is available in EEA on desktop/mobile. A tile links directly to its source site.
Ordering uses Search ranking algorithms with location/language relevance and the stated non-discriminatory principles.
Eligibility requires serving EEA users, relevant content and authoritative or specialist provider status.
This specific feature needs no new structured data or special feed. Eligible providers can express interest through the linked form.

chapters.title: Job sites: aggregator carousel and refinement chip
notes: Job-site features consist of an aggregator carousel and a refinement chip for job queries in EEA.
The carousel offers top aggregator results and More sites; the chip focuses results on aggregator text listings.
No added markup is required for these two features. This page is separate from JobPosting rich-result requirements.
Businesses serving EEA users can express interest through the linked form; that step is not an automatic appearance guarantee.

chapters.title: Places sites: aggregator carousel and refinement chip
notes: The current Places sites guide describes an aggregator carousel and refinement chip for Türkiye hotel and local-business queries.
The carousel links to relevant aggregator sites and More sites; the chip narrows the view to aggregator text results.
No added markup is required for this particular carousel/chip experience.
Businesses serving Türkiye users can express interest through the documented route. Avoid carrying over an old region assumption from another feature.

chapters.title: Search experiences in South Africa: badge and refinement chip
notes: The South African badge and refinement chip aim to help users find eligible South African platforms.
The badge can appear for applicable organic web results and ads; it explicitly does not change ranking.
Organic badge categories include travel, car hire, bus booking, products and food delivery. Ad support covers travel and shopping for eligible platforms.
The refinement chip filters toward eligible South African travel/shopping platforms; they need no added markup for the chip.
These features are limited to eligible South African sites; the interest form is a participation route rather than a worldwide SEO tactic.

chapters.title: Structured data carousels (beta)
notes: This beta is a single-site horizontal host carousel, distinct from a multi-provider aggregator unit. It uses ItemList with LocalBusiness/subtypes, Product or Event entities.

Current regions are EEA, Türkiye and South Africa on desktop/mobile, with category-specific lists. Türkiye covers hotels/vacation rentals/local businesses; other markets have broader listed travel, event and commerce categories.
Participation routes vary by category/region: general aggregator-interest, flight-interest, CSS program or South African feature-interest forms.
Use one summary/category page listing at least three entities and linking to standalone detail pages. An all-in-one page with only anchor destinations is unsupported.
Put the required markup on the summary page; detail-page markup is not mandatory for this beta. Include every listed item and every detail URL in the summary markup.
For paginated categories, add an ItemList for the items on each page. For infinite scroll, mark the entities initially loaded in the viewport.
ItemList requires itemListElement entries, item objects of an accepted type and 1-based position values. The declared order controls tile order.
Each item requires image, name and a canonical detail-page url. URLs must be unique and within the documented same-domain/subdomain/superdomain relationship.
Images must represent the item, be crawlable/indexable and use supported formats. Do not use logos; recommended multiple high-resolution crops are 16:9, 4:3 and 1:1 with at least 50K pixels.

Ratings are recommended, not common required properties. Numeric scales default to five points; use the documented best/worst values for other scales, fractions/percentages imply their scale, and decimal values use a dot.

LocalBusiness priceRange must be shorter than 12 characters to display. LodgingBusiness can use amenityFeature, and servesCuisine is for restaurants only. Generic types are permitted, but type-specific recommended properties require their appropriate type.
Product/Event offers can use Offer or AggregateOffer: a single price uses price, a range uses lowPrice/highPrice; do not provide incompatible single/range representations together.
priceCurrency uses three-letter ISO 4217; this guide defaults missing currency to USD. Event prices include required fees/charges, stay current and use zero for genuinely free events.
Validate technical markup with Rich Results Test, verify deployed access and rendered output with URL Inspection, then allow recrawl. Syntax validation cannot prove all content/policy quality.

Supported types and every property table/example are preserved in the source reference. Extra fields are allowed but might not display. A structured-data manual action can suppress the rich presentation without necessarily removing ordinary Search eligibility.

headings.text: Common list item properties ( LocalBusiness , Product, or Event )

chapters.title: Add a Search profile badge to your website
notes: A Search profile collects a publisher/creator's linked website and social-platform content in one Google destination.
Users following the profile may see more of its linked content on Discover; this differs from a Preferred Sources badge for Top Stories/AI features.
Claim the profile, obtain its profile.google.com/@handle URL and link from the site with the supplied badge or a text alternative.
Preserve official icon colors/proportions/orientation and consistent monochrome/color styling; downloaded assets and brand rules apply.
Touch targets should be at least 48×48 dp on Android and 44×44 px on iOS/web.
When using both profile and Preferred Sources promotions, use the higher-emphasis labeled profile button, not the bare Super G icon, to keep their functions clear.
The page gives an official help-community troubleshooting route; adding the badge is reader navigation, not a stated general ranking signal.

headings.text: How Search profiles work on Google
Add a Search profile badge to your website
Follow brand guidelines and best practices

chapters.title: Provide a site name to Google Search
notes: A site name identifies the whole site; a title link describes an individual page. Names are automated from homepage information and references elsewhere on the web.

Available in all Search languages on mobile and desktop, with one name per domain or subdomain. Subdirectories cannot have separate names; www and m subdomains are generally treated as equivalent to the domain.
WebSite structured data on the root homepage is the most important preference signal. Google also considers og:site_name, the title element, headings and other homepage text.

Choose a unique, accurate, concise, commonly recognized name; avoid misleading or generic keyword names. Keep homepage signals consistent. Long names can truncate; there is no documented fixed character limit.
Required WebSite properties are name and url, with url set to the canonical root homepage. Do not place the markup only on an interior page or repeat it unnecessarily on every page.

The homepage must be accessible to Google. Use identical site-name markup on duplicate HTTP/HTTPS or www/non-www homepages, and add these properties to an existing WebSite node rather than creating a second one.
alternateName is optional and can contain multiple alternatives in preference order, including acronyms, shorter brands and a lowercase domain/subdomain fallback.

Use Schema Markup Validator for syntax and URL Inspection for Google's access/rendering. Rich Results Test does not support site names. Request recrawling and allow days to weeks; internal pages also need processing.

If the chosen name differs: verify required markup, content policies, consistency, root location, crawlability and redirects. An accessible redirect target determines the name; a domain name can be a last-resort preference. There is no manual change or guaranteed selection.
Without subdomain homepage markup, the domain name may be used as fallback. The Google help community is the final documented troubleshooting route.

headings.text: How site names in Google Search are created
How to add a site name with structured data
What to do if your preferred site name isn't selected

chapters.title: Sitelinks
notes: Sitelinks are same-domain links clustered under a text result, selected automatically from site link structure to help users find shortcuts.
They appear only when Google judges them useful and query-relevant; unsuitable structure or weak relevance can mean none are shown.
Improve informative, relevant, compact page titles and headings; maintain logical navigation; link important pages from relevant pages; use concise relevant anchors; avoid repetitive content.

There is no documented manual selection mechanism. To remove an unwanted destination, Google suggests removing the page or applying noindex; consider the effect on that page's ordinary Search visibility as well.

chapters.title: Control your snippets in search results
notes: Snippets summarize a result. They are automated primarily from page content, vary by query, and may use the meta description when it provides a better description; Google cannot manually change individual snippets.
nosnippet suppresses snippets, max-snippet supplies a maximum text length, and data-nosnippet excludes specified page portions.
Meta descriptions should summarize the specific page accurately and persuasively. There is no Google-mandated fixed character limit; displayed snippets can truncate to device width.
Prefer unique page descriptions; a broader site description fits a homepage or aggregation page. If time is limited, prioritize the homepage and other important/popular URLs.
Descriptions can contain relevant labeled facts such as author, publication date, price, manufacturer or book length; they need not be written as a single sentence.
Database-driven sites can generate descriptions programmatically using actual page-specific data. They should be human-readable, diverse and useful; long keyword lists are poor substitutes.
The examples contrast keyword lists, repeated generic news copy, unrelated personal anecdotes and overly brief product text with specific summaries and helpful details.

A Read more deep link can lead from a snippet to a page section. Keep the target content immediately visible, avoid forced scroll position on load, and preserve URL hash fragments when using History API or window.location.hash.

headings.text: How to prevent snippets or adjust snippet length
Best practices for creating quality meta descriptions
Create unique descriptions for each page on your site
Include relevant information about the content in the description
Best practices for "Read more" deep links in Google Search

chapters.title: Introduction to structured data markup in Google Search
notes: Structured data provides standardized page information and can help Google understand entities/content and enable richer result appearances. Google's case studies are examples, not guaranteed performance lifts.

Put accurate markup on the page it describes; do not use a blank or content-invisible page as a container. Include all required properties and suitable recommended properties; fewer complete accurate fields beat inaccurate expansion.

Google Search Central documentation is definitive for Google's Search behavior even though most vocabulary comes from schema.org. Not every vocabulary property is needed for Google; data-vocabulary.org support is retired.

JSON-LD, Microdata and RDFa are supported. JSON-LD is recommended for easier maintenance, and Google can read dynamically injected JSON-LD in rendered content; properly implemented supported formats work.
Structured data must reflect visible content and meet general plus feature-specific policies. Passing tests cannot guarantee a rich result.
Develop with Rich Results Test, check deployed URLs and rich-result status reports in Search Console, and monitor errors/valid items.

A business experiment can compare selected stable pages before/after adding markup using Performance reports; pick nonseasonal pages, keep other changes limited and allow enough time, potentially several months, to reduce misleading comparisons.
The recipe example demonstrates how marked ingredients and preparation details give Google context; the complete original examples are retained in the reference.

headings.text: Why add structured data to a page?
How structured data works in Google Search
Measuring the effect of structured data

chapters.title: General structured data guidelines
notes: General guidelines plus the relevant feature guide determine rich-result eligibility. A passing Rich Results Test is insufficient because many quality/content issues are not easily testable.
A structured-data manual action can remove rich-result eligibility without changing ordinary web Search ranking; validate the distinction before describing it as a universal ranking penalty.

Valid markup may not show because context, user/location/device/history, page focus, hidden/misleading content, feature guidelines or other quality considerations affect display. Rich results are not guaranteed.
Use JSON-LD, Microdata or RDFa and keep relevant pages accessible: no robots blocking, noindex or login requirement that prevents Google from seeing them.
Content must be original where appropriate, relevant, current and visible. Avoid fake or misleading reviews, impersonation, deceptive engagement, spam and markup of irrelevant/off-topic content.
Include every required property and useful applicable recommendations; choose the most specific appropriate schema.org type. More fields alone do not prove compliance.
Put markup on the relevant page, including duplicate versions of that page, and use crawlable/indexable relevant image URLs when a feature requires images.

Multiple items can be nested or supplied separately. Related items can be connected with @id; supply the main content type and complete markup for visible items rather than describing a peripheral item alone.
Google checks spam/content policies and feature-specific restrictions in addition to syntax. The full list of quality headings and example cases remains in the reference.

chapters.title: Enriched search results
notes: Enriched search is a subset of rich results with added interaction, such as filtering job, recipe or event lists through supported attributes.

Each applicable result is a complete main content item on a leaf/detail page rather than a category/listing page. This instruction is feature-specific; the regional beta host carousel instead requires a summary page.

Include all required properties. Completeness is explicitly called one of the most important enriched-search ranking signals. More appropriate accurate recommendations can improve that experience; do not invent values to make a record look complete.
Keep markup and content genuine, visible and complete, and avoid unrelated ancillary markup masquerading as a main result. Follow general structured-data and feature-specific content guidelines.
Duplicates and large-scale poor-quality records can harm eligibility: Google may exclude an entire site from enriched results if a large proportion of its data is deficient.
An identical job offered at multiple real locations is not automatically duplicate content simply because the descriptions match; preserve genuine location distinctions.
These requirements concern eligibility/ranking within enriched features, not a promised boost to ordinary web rankings or a guarantee of display.

chapters.title: Generate structured data with JavaScript
notes: Google can process structured data present in the rendered DOM. Supported approaches include Google Tag Manager, custom JavaScript, server-side rendering and a CMS/plugin implementation.

In GTM, a custom HTML tag can inject a JSON-LD script. Use variables populated from the page data to avoid maintaining separate hard-coded values that diverge from visible content; publish after testing.

Custom JavaScript can fetch page-specific structured information and append a script element containing the returned structured-data text to the document. The source includes an API-fetch implementation example.

JavaScript-generated Product markup can make shopping crawls less frequent or reliable, especially for rapidly changing price/availability. Plan server resources and implementation accordingly rather than assuming all JS markup performs identically.
Rich Results Test URL input is recommended for JavaScript implementations; code-input testing has JavaScript/CORS and browser-context limitations.

Test the deployed rendered page and resolve missing/incorrect properties and syntax errors. A valid/eligible message does not guarantee that a feature will show; unsupported types may require rendered-DOM inspection instead of rich-result validation.

headings.text: Use Google Tag Manager to generate JSON-LD dynamically
Using variables in Google Tag Manager
Generate structured data with custom JavaScript

chapters.title: Structured data markup that Google Search supports
notes: The Search gallery is the current feature directory, with preview images and links to detailed implementation guides. Most supported features can be validated with Rich Results Test; not every schema.org type or Google appearance feature is supported by that tool.

Current listed features are Article, Breadcrumb, Carousel, Course list, Dataset, Discussion forum, Education Q&A, Employer aggregate rating, Event, Image metadata, Job posting, Local business, Math solver, Movie, Organization, Product, Profile page, Q&A, Recipe, Review snippet, Software app, Speakable, Subscription/paywalled content, Vacation rental and Video.
The traditional Carousel entry describes Recipe, Course list, Restaurant and Movie markup; this is distinct from the separate regional beta ItemList carousel guide.

Product can surface price, availability and review information. Organization can support identification/logos/administrative details; Profile page concerns creator profiles and is not the same as adding a Search profile follow badge.
FAQ and HowTo are not in this current gallery. Do not prepare from an old supported-feature checklist; absence alone is not a claim that every corresponding schema.org type is invalid vocabulary.
Use the detailed linked guide for each feature's required/recommended properties, content rules and availability; this gallery does not reproduce every subguide's specification.

chapters.title: Influencing your title links in search results
notes: Title links identify a result and influence how users understand relevance and decide to click. Google generates them automatically; the title element expresses a preference rather than an exact display instruction.

Give every page a descriptive concise title. Avoid vague Home/Profile labels, unnecessary verbosity, keyword repetition, whole-site boilerplate and micro-boilerplate that hides distinctions such as seasons or product variants.

There is no documented fixed title-element character limit; displayed title links truncate as needed for device width. Concise branding with a delimiter is useful, but a repeated brand may be omitted when already shown as the site name.
Make the main visual title distinct and prominent, with a clear main heading. Multiple equally prominent titles can cause confusion and Google may choose the first.
Keep the title's language and writing system aligned with primary page content; a mismatch, including transliteration, can lead Google to choose different text.
Google considers title element, visible title, headings, og:title, prominent other text, on-page anchors, incoming link text and WebSite structured data.

Crawling access matters: robots.txt can block content yet leave the URL indexed, causing Google to rely on off-page anchors. Use noindex when the goal is preventing indexing and ensure Google can see the rule.
Flight prices change rapidly, so Google recommends omitting them from title elements and likely suppresses them in generated title links.
Common rewrite reasons: half-empty title, obsolete dates, inaccurate scope, duplicate micro-boilerplate, no clear main title, language/script mismatch and repeated site names.

Updates require recrawling and processing, often days to weeks. Google cannot manually change an individual site's title links; investigate page issues, query relevance and the help community if needed.

chapters.title: Translated results in Google Search
notes: Google can translate title links/snippets to fill local-language content gaps. Clicking a translated result opens a machine-translated version, with options to access the original result/page.

Available on mobile and desktop in Arabic, Bengali, English, French, German, Gujarati, Hindi, Indonesian, Kannada, Korean, Malayalam, Marathi, Persian, Portuguese, Spanish, Tamil, Telugu, Thai, Turkish, Urdu and Vietnamese.

Google says it does not host translated pages; the behavior is similar to opening through Google Translate or browser translation. JavaScript and embedded images usually work, but ad networks may need URL handling changes.
No opt-in action is needed; applicability depends on user language. Monitor clicks/impressions with the Search Appearance filter in Search Console Performance.
To opt out of all Google Search translation features, use notranslate in robots/googlebot metadata or an X-Robots-Tag HTTP header. This is a translation control, not an indexing block.

If encoding 1 is listed and the name starts 1-, remove that prefix. If encoding 0 is listed and it starts 0-, remove it and set the internationalized-domain flag.

chapters.title: Video SEO best practices
notes: Videos can appear in main Search, Video mode, Images and Discover. Discovery, watch-page indexing, video indexing and specific rich-feature serving are separate stages.

Use recognizable video/embed/iframe/object containers. JavaScript videos must exist in rendered HTML; keep a container even when media APIs fail. Do not require clicks/swipes/typing to load the video or fragment-only URLs to locate it.
Structured data, video sitemaps and Open Graph metadata help discovery. An indexed well-performing watch page does not automatically mean its embedded video is indexed.

A watch page's main purpose is viewing one video. News video pages, episodes and highlights fit; complementary product demos, review trailers or categories of equal videos do not. Non-watch pages can still qualify for text/image results with a video badge.

Give each watch page a unique title/description. A video can appear on both a watch page and a complementary article; third-party embeds can be indexed on both the publisher page and the host's own page if each qualifies.
Google lists 3GP, 3G2, ASF, AVI, DivX, M2V, M3U, M3U8, M4V, MKV, MOV, MP4, MPEG, OGV, QVT, RAM, RM, VOB, WebM, WMV and XAP. Data URLs are unsupported.

Use a unique stable thumbnail URL per video; stable file URLs support previews/key moments and processing. Expiring CDN URLs can prevent indexing. Verified Googlebot can receive stable access where needed.
Distinguish watch-page URL (sitemap loc), player URL (embedUrl/player_loc) and actual file URL (contentUrl/content_loc). They describe different resources.

Thumbnail preferences can come from poster, thumbnail_loc/media:thumbnail, thumbnailUrl or og:video:image; keep the same URL across sources. Supported images: BMP/GIF/JPEG/PNG/WebP/SVG/AVIF, at least 60×30 pixels, preferably larger, accessible to Googlebot and Googlebot Images. At least 80% of pixels need alpha greater than 250.
Structured metadata must match the real video and other metadata; provide unique thumbnailUrl, name and description. Paid access should use appropriate paywall markup so Google can find the video.
Video previews require fetching actual video bytes; max-video-preview controls maximum preview duration. Markup does not guarantee a feature on every query.

Key moments may be automatic. Publisher Clip segments give labels/start/end times in all Search languages; SeekToAction supplies a timestamp URL pattern in the listed 12 languages. YouTube descriptions can supply timestamps/labels. nosnippet opts out of key moments, including automatic ones.

BroadcastEvent can enable a LIVE badge. For previews/key moments allow file/stream crawling, including M3U8, use stable supported contentUrl, and ensure both page host and video server have capacity. Verify CDN ownership if seeking crawl-error reports for its URL space.

For urgent removal request removal of the watch page; make it permanent with 404, noindex or authentication. Other embedding pages require their own actions. A past expires/expiration_date suppresses video results while the page can remain a text result; omit expiry for nonexpiring videos.

Geographic restrictions use regionsAllowed or ineligibleRegion, or one sitemap restriction with ISO country codes. allow with no countries means nowhere; deny with none means everywhere. Omit restrictions when none apply.

SafeSearch depends on correct explicit-content labeling. Monitor Video indexing (video indexing reasons), Video rich results (markup), and Performance with Videos Search appearance (visibility); troubleshoot with the relevant report and URL Inspection.

notes: This illustrated terminology guide covers text results, rich results, image results, video results and exploration features. UI appearance varies with time, device, country, language and query; not every result contains every possible element.

Attribution identifies the source through site name, favicon and visible URL. The visible URL consists of domain plus breadcrumb; breadcrumb reflects site hierarchy and can be supported by Breadcrumb markup.
Text results (formerly web results/plain blue links) can include attribution, title link, snippet, byline date, sitelinks, a text-result image and rich attributes.
Sitelinks groups contain two or more shortcuts and can link to pages, headings or anchors, including localized variants. They are selected automatically.
A text-result image is the relevant page image for the query and opens the embedding page; rich attributes such as ratings/recipe information commonly rely on structured data.

Image results contain thumbnails and attribution; the guide says image-thumbnail clicks go to the image. Video results contain thumbnail, title, attribution and upload date; a video-thumbnail click goes to the embedding webpage.
Byline dates are Google's estimated publication/update dates; video upload dates come from metadata. Use the linked feature guides for actual optimization rules.

Exploration features include related searches and related questions/People Also Ask. Searches are generated from the initial query and other users' searches; expanded questions show a featured snippet. Publishers cannot directly choose these suggestions.
Original annotated illustrations are linked in the source library so you can check each term visually without changing Google's diagrams.

chapters.title: Enable Web Stories on Google
notes: Web Stories are tappable/swipeable web pages blending video, audio, images, animation and text. Normal web-page SEO still applies.

Search single-result availability covers all Search regions/languages. Discover single-card availability covers Discover regions/languages and is most likely in the United States, India and Brazil; do not treat this as a guaranteed carousel everywhere.
Build with a story editor or AMP engineering, test device layouts with Chrome DevTools and follow the dedicated creation guidance.
A Story must be valid AMP. Validate with the Web Stories Google Test Tool, URL Inspection or AMP Linter; technical validity alone does not promise indexing or serving.
Required preview metadata on every story: publisher-logo-src, poster-portrait-src, title and publisher. Inspect the actual preview in the Story test tool.

Check indexing with URL Inspection, Page Indexing and Sitemaps reports; add site links or a sitemap for discovery. Every Story must have a self-referencing canonical and must not be blocked by robots.txt/noindex.
Declare language variants appropriately and comply with content policies; examples and linked resources are preserved in the reference.

chapters.title: Best practices for creating Web Stories
notes: Critical storytelling favors video; recommended storytelling adds a relatable perspective and a narrative arc with context, suspense and payoff.

Critical design advice recommends approximately 280 characters per page, visible unblocked text and restrained animation. The separate content-policy page warns that a majority of pages over 180 characters may lose eligibility for richer experiences; these are different stated thresholds, so use the stricter policy when eligibility matters.
Recommended design: Web Stories-appropriate calls to action, full-bleed high-quality assets, cover-page logo, brief videos, good balanced audio and optional auto-advance for video-only stories.

Video guidance recommends under 15 seconds per page, or 60 seconds maximum; audio should be high quality, at least 5 seconds, with clear speech. The policy page separately encourages videos under 60 seconds.
SEO fundamentals still apply: useful complete content, discoverable/indexable URLs, sitemap discovery, self-canonicals and localized-language handling.

Story titles must be shorter than 90 characters; a descriptive title shorter than 70 is recommended. This Story-specific rule is distinct from the general Search title guide's absence of a fixed title-element limit.

Attach AMP story metadata and ordinary page markup (title/description, structured data, Open Graph and Twitter cards). Recommendations include alt text, appropriate structured data and integrating Story links into homepage/category navigation.
URLs do not need a special stories/amp naming convention; use a coherent site URL strategy. Story page attachments can add depth without withholding the essential narrative.

Add accessible captions/subtitles, avoid burned-in text, and use semantic HTML. If the editor exports every slide as a video with baked-in text, the guide recommends the precise visible text as amp-video's title attribute only when semantic markup is unavailable.

Add landscape support for desktop appearance. Valid AMP is required; poster-portrait-src should be at least 640×853 with 3:4 ratio, and publisher-logo-src at least 96×96 with 1:1 ratio. Avoid text baked into the poster; og:image is recommended.
This page retains the older Index Coverage Report term; the newer enablement guide names Page Indexing. Use the current Search Console report name in practice.

chapters.title: Web Story Content Policies on Google
notes: Single-result Stories must satisfy Discover policies, Search Essentials and overall Search policies. Richer experiences additionally require Search Feature policies plus the listed Story content rules.
Egregious violations can permanently exclude a site from richer Story experiences; do not confuse this statement with guaranteed removal from all ordinary web results.
Copyright: Stories should be original or use material with permission; Google does not obtain rights for creators and may block infringing Stories.

Text-heavy Stories may be ineligible if most pages exceed 180 characters. Bite-sized video under 60 seconds per page is encouraged; keep this policy separate from the creation guide's 280-character advice.
Poor-quality stretched/pixelated assets and missing narrative/theme are prohibited. Stories must be complete and must not require external clicks to get essential information.
Stories whose sole goal is advertising are disallowed. Affiliate links may occupy a minor part, display ads must follow Story Ad Guidelines, and affiliate programs must follow Search spam policies.

chapters.title: Package tracking Early Adopters Program
notes: Package tracking is an API-backed Search experience where a user enters a package ID and Google retrieves the carrier's tracking information. It is not described as a schema.org-only integration.
The feature is available in all Search countries/languages, but the Early Adopters Program is no longer accepting new partners. Do not propose a currently open application path.
API expectations: almost no downtime, average response within 700 ms and 95th percentile no more than 1,000 ms. Failure can stop display of the carrier's tracking information.
Required field CurrentStatus includes current status, when it became valid, and error states.
Recommended fields: DeliveredDate, PromisedDate, TrackingNumber, TrackingURL, SupportPhoneNumbers, TransitEvents, CreateDate, PickupDate, TimestampEvent, LocationEvent and CanReschedule.

TransitEvents describe interim journey events, including date/time and applicable city/state/country. Region-specific support numbers and rescheduling status are recommended; these are not a license to share recipient data.
Google does not accept personal data or geographical information about the recipient or sender. Distinguish transit-event location from identifying a person's address/location.

questions.question: What does SEO actually do according to this guide?
questions.answer: It helps search engines understand content and helps people discover the website and decide whether to visit. I apply it to useful content, with technical access and a clear search presentation.

evidence.title: Search Engine Optimization (SEO) Starter Guide
evidence.quote: When you built your website, you likely created it with your users in mind, trying to make it easy for them to find and explore your content. One of those users is a search engine, which helps people discover your content. SEO—short for search engine optimization—is about helping search engines understand your content, and helping users find your site and make a decision about whether they should visit your site through a search engine.

questions.question: How long should we wait to evaluate an SEO change?
questions.answer: Google says effects can take hours to months, and generally advises waiting a few weeks to assess benefit. I establish a baseline and allow time for recrawling and processing; I do not promise an exact improvement date.

evidence.title: Search Engine Optimization (SEO) Starter Guide
evidence.section: How long until I see impact in search results?
evidence.quote: Every change you make will take some time to be reflected on Google's end. Some changes might take effect in a few hours, others could take several months. In general, you likely want to wait a few weeks to assess whether your work had beneficial effects in Google Search results. Keep in mind that not all changes you make to your website will result in noticeable impact in search results; if you're not satisfied with your results and your business strategies allow it, try iterating with the changes and see if they make a difference.

questions.question: Does every website need a sitemap to rank?
questions.answer: No. Google can discover pages through links, and the Starter Guide calls a sitemap optional. It is useful for communicating important URLs, particularly when discovery through links is weaker, but does not guarantee indexing.

evidence.title: Search Engine Optimization (SEO) Starter Guide
evidence.quote: If you're open to a little technical challenge, you could also submit a sitemap —which is a file that contains all the URLs on your site that you care about. Some content management systems (CMS) may even do this automatically for you. However this isn't required, and you should first focus on making sure people know about your site .

questions.question: How would you check whether Google can see a page properly?
questions.answer: Use URL Inspection to examine the rendered page and accessibility of its resources. Check CSS and JavaScript blocking and location-dependent responses, rather than trusting only my browser view.

evidence.title: Search Engine Optimization (SEO) Starter Guide
evidence.section: Check if Google can see your page the same way a user does
evidence.quote: When Google crawls a page, it should ideally see the page the same way an average user does . For this, Google needs to be able to access the same resources as the user's browser. If your site is hiding important components that make up your website (like CSS and JavaScript ), Google might not be able to understand your pages, which means they might not show up in search results or rank well for the terms you're targeting.

evidence.title: Search Engine Optimization (SEO) Starter Guide
evidence.section: Check if Google can see your page the same way a user does
evidence.quote: To check how Google sees your page, use the URL Inspection Tool in Search Console .

questions.question: Why organize related URLs into directories?
questions.answer: For users, it clarifies structure. At larger scale, it can help Google learn that different groups change at different frequencies. It is not a reason to rebuild every healthy site immediately.

evidence.title: Search Engine Optimization (SEO) Starter Guide
evidence.section: Group topically similar pages in directories
evidence.quote: If you have more than a few thousand URLs on your site, how you organize your content may have effects on how Google crawls and indexes your site. Specifically, using directories (or folders) to group similar topics can help Google learn how often the URLs in individual directories change.

evidence.title: Search Engine Optimization (SEO) Starter Guide
evidence.section: Group topically similar pages in directories
evidence.quote: The content in the policies directory seldomly changes, however the content in the promotions directory likely changes very often. Google can learn this information and crawl the different directories at different frequencies. To learn more about search-friendly site structures, check out our guide for ecommerce sites , for which a good URL structure is more important as they tend to be larger.

questions.question: Will duplicate product URLs trigger a duplicate-content penalty?
questions.answer: Routine duplication on one's own site is not itself a spam violation or cause of a manual action. I consolidate where appropriate because duplicates can confuse users and waste crawling, and distinguish this from copied or manipulative content.

evidence.title: Search Engine Optimization (SEO) Starter Guide
evidence.quote: Having duplicate content on your site is not a violation of our spam policies, but it can be a bad user experience and search engines might waste crawling resources on URLs that you don't even care about. If you're feeling adventurous, it's worth figuring out if you can specify a canonical version for your pages. But if you don't canonicalize your URLs yourself, Google will try to automatically do it for you.

questions.question: When would you choose a redirect rather than a canonical tag?
questions.answer: Use a redirect when the redundant URL should send users to the preferred page. If the alternate URL needs to remain accessible, a canonical declaration can indicate the preferred representative. Google ultimately performs canonical selection.

evidence.title: Search Engine Optimization (SEO) Starter Guide
evidence.quote: If you have multiple pages that have the same information, try setting up a redirect from non-preferred URLs to a URL that best represents that information. If you can't redirect, use the rel="canonical" link element instead. But again, don't worry too much about this; search engines can generally figure this out for you on their own most of the time.

questions.question: Must I include every exact keyword variation?
questions.answer: No. Understand audience language and use relevant terminology naturally. Google's language matching can relate a page to queries without every exact phrase appearing.

evidence.title: Search Engine Optimization (SEO) Starter Guide
evidence.quote: However, don't worry if you don't anticipate every variation of how someone might seek your content. Google's language matching systems are sophisticated and can understand how your page relates to many queries, even if you don't explicitly use the exact terms in them.

questions.question: Does Google always show the title and meta description we write?
questions.answer: No. Title links have several inputs, including title elements and headings; snippets usually come from page text and can sometimes use a meta description. I improve accurate inputs and inspect actual presentation.

evidence.title: Search Engine Optimization (SEO) Starter Guide
evidence.quote: The title link is the headline part of the search result and it can help people decide which search result to click. There are a few sources that Google uses to generate this title link, including the words inside the <title> element (also called the title text) and other headings on the page. This title text can also be used for the title that's shown in browsers and bookmarks.

evidence.title: Search Engine Optimization (SEO) Starter Guide
evidence.quote: The snippet is sourced from the actual content of the page the search result is linking to, thus you have complete control over the words that can be used to generate the snippet. Occasionally the snippet may be sourced from the contents of the meta description tag, which is typically a succinct, one- or two-sentence summary of the page. A good meta description is short, unique to one particular page, and includes the most relevant points of the page. Check out our tips for writing good meta descriptions for more inspiration.

questions.question: What makes a good image optimization answer?
questions.answer: Sharp relevant images placed near explanatory text, with descriptive alt text explaining their relationship to the page. The guide focuses on discoverability and understanding, not a prescribed keyword density.

evidence.title: Search Engine Optimization (SEO) Starter Guide
evidence.section: Add high-quality images near relevant text
evidence.quote: Use images that are sharp and clear, and place them near text that's relevant to the image. The text that's near images can help Google better understand what the image is about and what it means in context to your page.

evidence.title: Search Engine Optimization (SEO) Starter Guide
evidence.section: Add descriptive alt text to the image
evidence.quote: Alt text is a short, but descriptive piece of text that explains the relationship between the image and your content. It helps search engines understand what your image is about and the context of how your image relates to your page, so writing good alt text is quite important. You can add this to your HTML with the alt attribute of the img element, or your CMS may

questions.question: How would you optimize a video page from this guide?
questions.answer: Create a high-quality video, give it a standalone page where the video is the main focus, add relevant supporting text, and write descriptive video titles and descriptions. Then consult Google's video-specific guidance.

evidence.title: Search Engine Optimization (SEO) Starter Guide
evidence.quote: Create high-quality video content, and embed the video on a standalone page, near text that's relevant to that video.

evidence.title: Search Engine Optimization (SEO) Starter Guide
evidence.quote: Write descriptive text in the titles and description fields of a video (the title of a video is still a title, and so you can apply the best practices for writing titles here too).

questions.question: Should we add nofollow to all external links?
questions.answer: The guide recommends linking to trusted relevant resources normally and qualifying links you cannot endorse or that come from users. Additional official guidance prefers sponsored for paid placements and ugc for user contributions.

evidence.title: Search Engine Optimization (SEO) Starter Guide
evidence.quote: Links can provide more context on a topic, both for users and search engines, which may help demonstrate your knowledge on a topic. However when you're linking to pages outside of your control, for example content on other sites, make sure you trust the resource you're linking to. If you can't trust the content and you still want to link to them, add a nofollow or

questions.question: Is PageRank still relevant, and is it the whole ranking system?
questions.answer: It remains one fundamental algorithm involving links, but Google uses many signals. Treating rankings as a PageRank-only problem misses relevance, quality, and the wider search process.

questions.question: Can a paid promotion campaign directly buy organic ranking?
questions.answer: No. Legitimate promotion can improve awareness and discovery. Google does not accept money for organic inclusion, higher rankings, or faster crawling.

Google never accepts money to include or rank sites in our search results, and it costs nothing to appear in our organic search results. Resources such as Search Console , the official Google Search Central blog , and our discussion forum can provide you with a great deal of information about how to optimize your site for Google's non-advertising search results (often called "organic search").

questions.question: Explain how Google Search works in under a minute.
questions.answer: Google discovers URLs through known pages, links, and sitemaps. Googlebot may crawl and render them, including JavaScript. Google then analyzes content, groups similar pages and selects canonicals, and may store information in its index. For a query, it serves relevant, high-quality results based on many signals and user context. None of the stages is guaranteed.

evidence.title: In-depth guide to how Google Search works
evidence.section: Introducing the three stages of Google Search
evidence.quote: Crawling: Google downloads text, images, and videos from pages it found on the internet with automated programs called crawlers.

evidence.title: In-depth guide to how Google Search works
evidence.section: Introducing the three stages of Google Search
evidence.quote: Indexing: Google analyzes the text, images, and video files on the page, and stores the information in the Google index, which is a large database.

evidence.title: In-depth guide to how Google Search works
evidence.section: Introducing the three stages of Google Search
evidence.quote: Serving search results: When a user searches on Google, Google returns information that's relevant to the user's query.

questions.question: What is the difference between discovery and crawling?
questions.answer: Discovery means Google knows a URL exists. Crawling means it actually requests and downloads the content. A discovered URL can remain uncrawled because of scheduling, access restrictions, or server issues.

evidence.title: In-depth guide to how Google Search works
evidence.quote: The first stage is finding out what pages exist on the web. There isn't a central registry of all web pages, so Google must constantly look for new and updated pages and add them to its list of known pages. This process is called "URL discovery". Some pages are known because Google has already visited them. Other pages are discovered when Google extracts a link from

questions.question: Explain RAG in an SEO interview.
questions.answer: Retrieval-augmented generation grounds a response in relevant pages retrieved from the Search index, using Google's core systems. It can improve freshness and accuracy and provide supporting links, rather than relying entirely on a model's training memory.
